path.title: AI for Leaders
path.subtitle: Build a defensible AI bet portfolio without selling out the team
path.summary: Most leaders treat AI like a vibe; they pick a flagship feature, hand it to one team, and discover 11 months later that 87% of MVP 'AI features' never reach 1,000 users. This course teaches you to think about AI the way you think about a budget: as a portfolio of bets with explicit kill criteria, real eval gates, and a story your board will believe. By the end you can scope a 12-month AI bet portfolio, defend it line by line, and not flinch when the SVP asks 'what happens if it doesn't work?'.

lessons.title: What AI Actually Does for a Business
lessons.subtitle: Two curves shifted; everything else is just shopping

audioChapters.label: Mental model: two curves, not one wave

blocks.md:
Your CEO said the company is 'AI-first now.' The all-hands clapped. Engineering went back to their laptops. By Tuesday, three product managers had drafted three different AI roadmaps; by Friday, two of them had quietly hired vendors.

This is what a strategy without a model looks like. The slogan is doing all the work. By the end of this lesson you will have a model with two axes that turns every AI conversation in your company into a structured one. You will also know which 80% of AI features at your company are theatre, and which 20% might be real.

blocks.title: Mental model: AI shifted two curves, not one wave
blocks.md:
Forget 'AI is a wave.' Waves do not give you decision rules.

**AI is two curves moving against each other.** Curve one is the *cost* of completing a unit of cognitive task — it has fallen roughly 90% in 24 months on most language tasks. Curve two is the *capability frontier* — the maximum task difficulty an off-the-shelf model can attempt with non-laughable accuracy. It has risen.

The area where these two curves intersect is the only strategically interesting region in your business. Outside that region, AI is irrelevant or unaffordable. Your job as a leader is not to chase the wave; it is to identify which of your problems just walked into the intersection.

blocks.caption: Watch the cost curve fall and the capability curve rise. Notice which problems pass through the intersection in 2024, in 2025, in 2026.

hi-IN.title: Founder ne deck mein ChatGPT screenshots daal diye
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. VC ne pucha — "AI strategy?" Founder ne deck mein **slide 7 pe ChatGPT ke screenshots** daal diye. Caption — "AI-powered customer success."

VC ne sirf ek question pucha — "kaunsi cost curve shift hui jo aapne notice kiya?" Slide 8 nahi tha. Founder ne kaha — "voh next milestone hai." Round closed. **Cheque nahi cuta.**

Moral: screenshot ke neeche curve nahi ho toh slide nahi, ad hai.

en.title: The deck without the curve
en.md: Founder pitches an 'AI-powered' product. The deck has GPT screenshots. The VC asks one question: which curve shifted that made this possible now? There is no slide 8. The cheque does not clear. The lesson generalises beyond fundraising.

blocks.md:
Most of your team's AI ideas are not bad; they are *misallocated*. Eighty percent of them are about tasks where AI is technically possible but commercially uninteresting; the other twenty percent are about tasks where AI just became commercially possible for the first time.

The 80/20 capability lens is one question, asked twice, in this order:

1. **What is now feasible that was not feasible 18 months ago?** (Capability curve.)
2. **At what cost?** (Cost curve.)

If you cannot answer question 1 in a sentence, the idea is theatre. If question 1 has an answer but question 2 does not, the idea is a research project, not a product. Both go to the bottom of the stack.

A crisp number for the lens: at a Bengaluru SaaS series-B I worked with in 2026, this single question killed 19 of 23 proposed AI features in a 90-minute review and saved roughly ₹1.7 crore in build cost.

blocks.title: Translation moment — 'we should use AI for support' becomes a strategy bullet

steps.label: Step 1 — The English question
steps.body: Director of CX says: 'We should use AI for customer support.' Sounds reasonable. Means almost nothing.

steps.label: Step 2 — Curve check (capability)
steps.body: Ask: what is now feasible? 'Drafting responses to ambiguous tickets in passable English' became feasible in 2024. 'Resolving complex billing disputes end-to-end' did not.

steps.label: Step 3 — Curve check (cost)
steps.body: Ask: at what cost? Drafting at ~₹0.40 per ticket vs an agent at ₹38. Ratio is 95:1, well past the 'commercially interesting' threshold.

steps.label: Step 4 — Scope the surface
steps.body: Restate as: 'Draft first-response for tier-1 tickets in English-only categories. Agent edits before send. Tier-2 unchanged.' This is now a feature spec, not a slogan.

steps.label: Step 5 — Tag the assumption
steps.body: Write down: 'We assume our tier-1 ticket mix is >60% English-only and that draft acceptance is >55%. We will know by day 45.' This goes into the assumption ledger you will build in lesson 5.

blocks.prompt: Your CTO suggests building 'an AI tutor that answers any student question in any language with full personalisation.' What is the leadership-grade response?

choices.label: Ask which capability shift made this feasible in the last 18 months — and which sub-task is now under cost, separately.
choices.explain: Correct. You have just split a slogan into a capability question and a cost question. If the CTO can answer both, you have a feature; if not, you have a research project.

choices.label: Approve the spec; AI tutoring is the future of edtech.
choices.explain: Slogan-driven approval. 'Future of edtech' is true and useless; it does not tell you which sub-task to fund.

choices.label: Reject the idea; AI tutors hallucinate.
choices.explain: Reasonable concern, wrong altitude. Hallucination is a property of the implementation; a scoped sub-task with eval gates can keep it bounded. Premature rejection costs you the 20%.

choices.label: Hire a Chief AI Officer to evaluate.
choices.explain: Org-chart deflection. You can apply the 80/20 lens in the same meeting; outsourcing it adds three months and no information.

hi-IN.title: All-hands ke baad ka real scene
hi-IN.md:
CEO ne all-hands mein bola — "hum AI-first hain." Engineering ne lunch ke time pe pucha — "mtlb kya?" CTO bola — "matlab API access." Engineering ne dekha — **12 ghante ka rate-limit hai, sirf 4 prompts per minute, aur token budget mein lunch nahi aata.**

Slogan upar, capacity neeche. Curve shift hua tha, lekin company ke andar tak nahi pahuncha tha. Bhai, AI-first banne ka cost API quota hai, slide nahi.

en.title: Slogan up top, capacity at the bottom
en.md: The CEO declared 'AI-first.' Engineering discovered that 'AI-first' meant a 4-prompts-per-minute rate limit and a token budget that didn't cover lunch. The capability curve had moved outside the company; it had not moved inside the company. Slogans cannot create capacity.

blocks.text: Move 2 — The 'what's now feasible that wasn't' question

blocks.md:
Move 2 is a habit, not a framework. Every time someone in your company proposes an AI feature, you ask one question, in exactly these words:

> *"What is now feasible that was not feasible 18 months ago — and how do we know?"*

The phrasing matters. Not 'is AI useful here?' (yes, always, vacuously). Not 'should we use AI?' (slogan). Not 'what is your roadmap?' (premature). The question forces the proposer to name a *delta in capability* and *cite evidence*. If they cannot, the conversation ends.

In six months of using this question at a Pune fintech, the leadership team killed roughly 60% of incoming AI proposals at the first meeting; the survivors had a notably higher production-deployment rate, around 73% versus 18% before.

coach.name: Board-Member Bharat
coach.role: Independent director, ex-CFO of a listed mid-cap, has watched four CEOs say 'AI-first' in the last 36 months

intro: Main aapko paanch AI proposals dikhata hoon — woh proposals jo aapke peers ne board ke saamne rakhe. Aap classify kijiye: **fund**, **wait**, **theatre**, ya **research**.
Spoiler — main inn proposals ko already dekh chuka hoon. Mera passing percentage 22% hai. Aap se umeed kam hai, but try toh kijiye.

scenarios.situation: D2C founder pitches: 'AI-powered personalised email recommendations for our 4 lakh subscribers. We will use GPT.' No baseline, no cohort, no curve cited.
scenarios.explain: Theatre. Personalised email recs have been industry-standard since 2014; no curve shifted. Adding 'GPT' is rebranding, not strategy. Kill at the first meeting.

scenarios.situation: Insurance company head of claims pitches: 'Use a multimodal model to read damage photos and pre-fill the claim form. Pilot on motor claims under ₹50,000. Eval set of 2,000 historical claims attached. Cost ~₹4 per claim vs ₹180 for the manual coder.'
scenarios.explain: Fund. Multimodal capability genuinely shifted in 2024; cost ratio 45:1; cohort is scoped; eval set exists. This is the 20%. Ship the pilot, attach a kill criterion.

scenarios.situation: EdTech head pitches: 'Build a fully personalised AI tutor that adapts to each child's learning pace across all 11 subjects in 7 languages.' No sub-task scoping; no eval; cited 'OpenAI is doing it'.
scenarios.explain: Theatre. Slogan-shaped scope, no curve evidence, no cohort. The 'OpenAI is doing it' is the giveaway: that is comparison-driven, not problem-driven. Kill it. (Note: a *scoped* version of this — 'hint generation for class-7 algebra word problems' — could have been fund-able. The pitch did not do the scoping work.)

scenarios.situation: CFO pitches: 'Use AI to fully automate our financial close. Replace 40% of the finance team in 9 months.' Cost-per-token math attached, but the eval set has 12 examples and the 'agent' has no fallback path.
scenarios.explain: Research. The capability is genuinely interesting; the cost math is plausible; but a 12-example eval set on a function with audit liability is reckless. Don't fund yet; revisit when there is a 500+ example eval set and a fallback path.

scenarios.situation: Head of Sales pitches: 'AI to score inbound leads and route them automatically.' Lead-scoring has worked at the company since 2017; the proposal cites no new capability shift.
scenarios.explain: Wait. Lead-scoring is the textbook 'no curve shifted' case. The existing model is fine; an LLM rewrite is mostly a project to keep someone employed. Revisit in 12 months when the cost falls another order of magnitude.

scenarios.situation: Hospital CTO pitches: 'AI to draft discharge summaries from doctor notes. Pilot on 1 ward, 3-month duration, eval against gold-standard human-written summaries on 800 cases. Disclaimer: the model is wrong on roughly 11% of summaries today.'
scenarios.explain: Research. The capability shifted, the cohort is right, the eval is real. But 11% wrong on a discharge summary is unsafe to ship as-is. Fund the next eval cycle, not the rollout. The honest disclosure of the failure rate is a good sign.

blocks.title: The classic trap: shiny demo, no measurable outcome
blocks.md:
The single most common failure pattern in 2024-26 leader AI programs: a team builds a demo, shows it at all-hands, gets applause, ships nothing.

The fix is not 'demand more demos.' The fix is **never let a demo end without a measurable outcome attached, in writing, before anyone leaves the room.** A demo without a cohort-scoped metric is a screensaver.

A crisp number from a 2026 Bengaluru SaaS post-mortem: 87% of internal AI demos that received standing applause never reached 1,000 users. The 13% that did had one thing in common — a cohort and a metric written on a slide *during* the demo, not after.

blocks.prompt: You're handed an AI feature proposal. Order the questions you ask, from first to last.

items.label: Which capability shifted in the last 18 months that makes this feasible now?
items.detail: If they cannot answer, the rest does not matter. Stop here.

items.label: What is the cost per task, and what is the manual baseline?
items.detail: If the ratio is < 5:1, the bet rarely survives 12 months.

items.label: Which user cohort do we test on, and how is it scoped?
items.detail: 'All users' is not a cohort. 'English-only tier-1 tickets in the first 30 days' is.

items.label: What's the 90-day kill criterion?
items.detail: Threshold + cohort + action. 'We'll revisit' does not count.

items.label: Who owns it, and where does the 'why' live?
items.detail: If only the AI team can articulate the user problem, the program is rudderless.

items.label: What goes into the assumption ledger?
items.detail: Five to seven dated assumptions; the bet is the conjunction of these holding.

blocks.hint: The earliest filters are cheapest. Curve check first; budget and ledger last.

blocks.instruction: Pick one AI idea floating around your company right now (your own, or someone else's). Apply the 'what's now feasible that wasn't' question. Write a 2-3 sentence answer naming (a) the specific capability shift, (b) the cost ratio against the manual baseline, and (c) the user cohort you would scope for the first 90 days. If you cannot answer (a), say so explicitly — that itself is useful information.
blocks.expected:
Strong answer (paraphrased example):

'(a) In late-2024, multimodal models reliably read low-resolution screenshots of receipts in mixed Hindi-English. (b) Our manual data-entry cost is ~₹22 per receipt; LLM cost is ~₹0.80, ratio ~27:1. (c) First 90 days: only motor-insurance claims under ₹25,000 from our top-3 distributor cities, with a hard fallback to manual entry on any low-confidence read.'

Weak answer pattern: 'AI is getting really good and we should use it for our forms.' (No capability shift named. No cost. No cohort. This is the 80%.)

blocks.prompt: Which of the following are signs an AI proposal lives in the 'theatre' quadrant? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: The proposal cites 'AI-first' or 'cutting-edge AI' but does not name which capability shifted.
choices.explain: Yes. Sloganeering without a named curve shift is the canonical theatre signature.

choices.label: The pilot is scoped to a specific user cohort with a 90-day metric.
choices.explain: Opposite. Cohort scoping with a metric is the signature of the *fund* quadrant, not theatre.

choices.label: The cost-per-task math is missing or hand-waved ('we'll figure it out').
choices.explain: Yes. Missing cost math means either no one did the work, or the work was done and the answer was bad. Either way, theatre.

choices.label: The eval set has 800+ representative examples and a known failure rate.
choices.explain: Strong signal of *research* or *fund*, not theatre. A real eval set is one of the most expensive artefacts to fake.

hi-IN.title: Mummy-aunty test for AI strategy
hi-IN.md:
Apni mummy ko 30 second mein samjhao — "company AI mein kya kar rahi hai." Agar tu bola — "hum AI-first hain, transformation chal raha hai" — mummy bolegi — "matlab kuch nahi."

Agar tu bola — "hum customer support ke top-1 tickets ke draft AI se likhwa rahe hain, isse roz 4 ghante bachte hain, agent edit karke send karta hai" — mummy bolegi — "theek hai, paisa bach raha hai toh accha hai."

Mummy nahi convince hui toh board nahi convince hoga. Mummy-aunty test pass kar.

en.title: The mummy-aunty test, generalised
en.md: Explain your AI strategy to a non-technical relative in 30 seconds. If you find yourself reaching for 'transformation' or 'AI-first', you have not finished thinking. Boards have a higher bar than your aunty, but the failure mode is identical.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Series-B That Demo'd 'AI Everywhere'
blocks.source: Anonymous Chief of Staff at a Series-B Bengaluru SaaS, ARR ~$22M
blocks.story:
On March 6, 2025, the CEO of a Bengaluru-based vertical SaaS company stood in front of his board and said the words every founder thinks will save them: *'AI everywhere.'* The deck had 41 slides. Eleven of them said the word 'agentic'. Three said 'transformational'. None of them had a number on them.

The board, charmed, approved a ₹9 crore AI line item for the year. The CEO went back and asked his VP of Engineering to 'figure out the roadmap'. The VP, who had never shipped an LLM feature, hired two ML engineers in Hyderabad at ₹65L each, bought enterprise OpenAI credits, and let every team add 'AI' to a Q2 OKR.

Eighteen months later, in October 2026, the audit came in. The company had shipped: an AI-powered email summarizer (turned off after 3 weeks because users complained), a 'Smart Search' that was just BM25 with a re-ranker, and a chatbot on the marketing site that the SDR team disabled because it was answering pricing questions wrong. Net new revenue attributable to AI: zero. Net new churn prevented: zero. Spend: ₹11.4 crore (140% of budget).

The board replaced the CEO in November. The new CEO's first slide at her first board meeting had three rows: *Bet 1, Bet 2, Bet 3*. Each had a number. Two of them were small.
blocks.takeaway: 'AI everywhere' is the strategic equivalent of 'we'll figure it out'. Boards don't fund vibes for 18 months in a row.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: Vikrant's Four Weeks to Scope
blocks.setup:
It's January 2026. **Vikrant**, VP of Product at a 300-person Bengaluru SaaS, has just been handed a board mandate: *'Build us an AI strategy. Q1.'* The CFO, who has seen this movie before, sends him a single Slack message: *'Vikrant — I will fund this. But I need ROI projections, not a deck. You have 4 weeks.'*

Vikrant has one analyst, a half-finished Notion page titled 'AI ideas (40+)', and a CFO who counts in basis points. His first instinct is to make a slide called 'AI Transformation Roadmap'. **Stop him.**

coach.name: CFO-Veteran Vinita
coach.role: Ex-CFO at two Indian unicorns, now operating advisor. Counts in cash, not capabilities.

stages.prompt: Vikrant opens his laptop on day 1 and asks: *'Where do I start?'* What do you tell him?

options.label: Start with a vision deck. 'AI-First [Company Name]' — get the board excited, then back-fill the substance.
options.explain: This is exactly the trap the Series-B above fell into. Vinita: *'Vikrant, the board doesn't need to be excited. They need to be reassured. Vision decks without numbers are just expensive screensavers.'*

options.label: Pick the 3-5 highest-leverage workflows in the company today, and ask: where would AI move a metric that already shows up on the P&L?
options.explain: **Yes.** Strategy starts from existing P&L lines. CAC, gross margin, sales cycle, support cost per ticket. If AI can move one of those by 15%+, you have a bet. If it can't, you don't.

options.label: Hire a McKinsey AI strategy engagement. They've done this for 200 companies.
options.explain: ₹3 crore for a deck you could write in 4 weeks if you talked to your own customers. Vinita: *'You're outsourcing the one thing the board hired YOU to do.'*

options.label: Survey all 300 employees: 'Where would AI help your job?'
options.explain: You'll get 300 answers, all valid, none prioritized. Internal demand surveys produce wishlists, not strategies. Save this for week 3 once you have a frame.

stages.prompt: Day 9. Vikrant has narrowed to 12 candidate use cases. The CFO is asking how he'll **rank** them. What's the frame?

options.label: Score each on (1) impact on a P&L line, (2) feasibility with current LLM tech in 2026, (3) data readiness. Three columns, one number each, sum.
options.explain: **Clean.** Three axes the CFO can audit. Impact = rupees. Feasibility = does this exist or are we inventing? Data readiness = do we have the inputs without a 6-month pipeline build? Boring scoring beats elegant theorizing.

options.label: Rank by 'strategic differentiation' — pick the bets that competitors can't easily copy.
options.explain: Differentiation matters in year 3. In year 1, you need bets that *work*. A defensible bet that doesn't ship is just a thesis. Ship first, defend second.

options.label: Rank by which features are most fun to demo. Demos drive sales.
options.explain: This is how you get the email summarizer that gets turned off in 3 weeks. Demos are not metrics.

options.label: Combine impact-on-P&L with a hard 'data readiness' filter — kill anything that needs a new data pipeline before it can ship.
options.explain: **Sharper.** Data readiness is the silent killer of AI roadmaps. Vinita: *'I've watched ₹4 crore of AI budget get spent building data pipelines for a feature that never shipped. Filter early.'*

stages.prompt: Day 21. Vikrant has 3 finalists. The CFO wants ROI projections. He's tempted to write *'$2M ARR uplift in year 1'* because it sounds bold. What do you tell him?

options.label: Write three numbers per bet: optimistic, base, pessimistic. Show the assumptions. Let the CFO pick which one she believes.
options.explain: **This is the move.** A range with assumptions is auditable. A point estimate is a hostage situation. Vinita will respect the range; she'll cross-examine the point estimate.

options.label: $2M ARR uplift, confidently. Boards reward boldness.
options.explain: Boards reward boldness *that ships*. You're 6 months from being the CEO who promised 40% CAC reduction and delivered 4%. Don't be that CEO. (See lesson 5.)

options.label: Refuse to project. Say 'AI is too uncertain to forecast.'
options.explain: The CFO will fund someone who *will* forecast. Refusing the question doesn't make it go away; it just makes you look unprepared.

options.label: Project the *cost* precisely (you control it) and the *uplift* as a range tied to a leading indicator you'll measure in 90 days.
options.explain: **Even better.** Tying uplift to a 90-day leading indicator (e.g., 'time-to-first-resolution drops by X') gives the CFO a checkpoint. If the indicator doesn't move, you kill the bet at month 4, not month 12.

stages.prompt: Day 27. Vikrant's draft strategy has 3 bets, ROI ranges, and 90-day leading indicators. He's about to present. What's the **one slide** the CFO needs to see first?

options.label: A diagram of the AI tech stack — vector DB, model layer, orchestration, eval framework.
options.explain: The CFO does not care about your tech stack on slide one. She cares whether this returns capital. Tech stack is slide 14.

options.label: A 3-row table: Bet | Investment | 90-day signal | Year-1 expected return (range). Then everything else.
options.explain: **Perfect.** Three rows, four columns, no jargon. Vinita: *'If I can read your strategy in 30 seconds, I'll fund it. If I need 30 minutes, I'll ask you to come back next quarter.'*

options.label: A market map of every AI competitor in your category.
options.explain: Useful context. Wrong slide one. The board hired you to make decisions, not to summarize the market.

options.label: A bold headline: 'How AI Will 10x [Company Name]' with a hero image.
options.explain: You just became the Series-B CEO from the field notes. The board has seen this slide before. They didn't fund it then either.

outcomes.perfect: Vinita pours you a coffee. Vikrant walks into the boardroom on day 28 with three bets, three numbers, and three checkpoints. The CFO funds all three. The board lets him keep his job. **You just turned a vision deck into a strategy.**
outcomes.good: Solid frame, mostly. Re-read the section on 90-day leading indicators — that's the difference between 'we have a strategy' and 'we have a strategy that survives quarter 2'.
outcomes.learn: You drifted toward vibes. The Series-B in the field notes did the same thing and lost a CEO over it. Re-read the lesson, especially the **three-axis scoring** and the **range-not-a-point-estimate** sections. Try again.

points: AI is two curves moving against each other — cost falling, capability rising. Strategy lives where they cross.
Most AI ideas at your company are theatre; the 80/20 lens kills them in one meeting.
Ask one question — 'what is now feasible that was not feasible 18 months ago, and how do we know?' — and ask it every time.
A demo without a cohort-scoped metric is a screensaver; never let a demo close without one.
If your strategy fails the mummy-aunty test, your board will not save you.

blocks.prompt: Pick the next AI proposal sitting in your inbox or your team's roadmap. Plot it on the 2x2 (capability shifted? cost OK?) and write one sentence on which quadrant it lives in. If it lands in 'fund', ask yourself why it is not already funded. If it lands in 'theatre', ask yourself why it is still on the roadmap.

blocks.md:
Your VP of Product walks in with a 14-page deck for The Flagship AI Feature. It will cost ₹2.4 crore. It will take 11 months. It will be 'transformative.' It has one team, one timeline, and one outcome.

This lesson is about why that deck, no matter how good, is the most expensive way to bet on AI. Not because the feature is wrong; because the *structure* is wrong. By the end, you will have a 3-bet portfolio template, a hypothesis register that fits on a single page, and a 90-day milestone gate that will make your less-attached self proud of your future-attached self for honouring it.

blocks.title: Mental model: a 3-bet portfolio with one slot you cannot yet fill
blocks.md:
AI bets are not equities. Returns are not continuous; they are mostly binary at the 90-day mark. **Concentration is therefore worse, not better, than diversification.** One bet means one shot at learning; if it fails, you have spent a year and learned only that this team, on this problem, with this scope, did not work. Three independent bets give you three signals.

The fourth slot — the one you reserve at ~15% and refuse to name — is the one most leaders skip. Don't. The capability curve will move during your year. The bet you should make in month 7 is not knowable in month 1. Reserve the right to be smarter later.

The pattern: **3 named bets + 1 reserved slot, sized unequally, each with a pre-committed 90-day kill criterion.** Anything else is hope, dressed up as a strategy.

hi-IN.title: Flagship feature ka flop — ek classic katha
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, ek SaaS company thi. Funded series-B. Founder ne board ko bola — "hum AI mein **flagship** banaa rahe hain." Naam tha — *NeuroAssist*. Roadmap 11 months. Budget ₹2.4 crore. Single team, 9 engineers, 1 PM.

Month 8 mein realize hua — model ka quality enough nahi hai shipping ke liye. Month 11 mein launch hua — 47 paying users. Total cost ₹2.6 crore (overshoot 8%). Founder ne board ko bola — "AI is a long game."

Agar woh paisa **3 bets** mein lagta — har 90 din mein gate hota — toh saal ke andar 2 dead-ends mar gaye hote, aur ek bet mein 8x return hota. Single bet ka problem yeh hai — saal khatam, learning zero.

en.title: The single-bet flop, in industry-neutral form
en.md: Series-B SaaS, ₹2.4 crore on one flagship AI feature, eleven-month roadmap, single team. Launches at month eleven; finds 47 paying users at month twelve. The lesson is not that AI is hard; it is that one bet means one outcome and one lesson. Three bets at the same total cost would have produced two early kills and one survivor — and your year of learning would have been compounded, not wasted.

blocks.md:
A hypothesis register is the single page that holds your AI program together. Every bet has one row. The columns are unforgiving:

- **The bet** (one sentence, names the user problem and the cohort).
- **The capability shift** (which curve moved, in one phrase).
- **Cost-per-task vs baseline** (a ratio).
- **The 90-day kill criterion** (cohort + threshold + action).
- **Owner** (one named human, not 'team').
- **Date of next review** (an actual date, not 'Q3').

If any column is empty, the bet does not exist yet. Sounds harsh; that is the point. The register is a forcing function, not a status report.

A crisp number from a Mumbai fintech in early 2026: introducing the register cut the average time-to-kill for failing AI bets from 9.5 months to 91 days, freeing roughly ₹4.1 crore of budget that previously rolled into 'continued exploration.'

blocks.title: Translation moment — 'we want to use AI in claims' becomes a register row

steps.label: Step 1 — The English question
steps.body: VP of Operations: 'We want to use AI in claims processing.' The deck has 11 slides. The register has zero rows so far.

steps.label: Step 2 — The bet column
steps.body: Forced into one sentence: 'Pre-fill the claim form for motor claims under ₹50,000 in our top-3 distributor cities.' Notice what got cut: 'fully automate claims' was the original ask. The register said no.

steps.label: Step 3 — The capability shift column
steps.body: 'Multimodal OCR on damage photos passed 92% accuracy on our internal eval as of February 2026.' One phrase. If this column is hand-wavy, the bet is research, not a bet.

steps.label: Step 4 — The cost ratio column
steps.body: Manual coder ₹180/claim. LLM ₹4/claim. Ratio 45:1. Anything under ~5:1 should make you nervous; anything under 1:1 should kill the bet on the spot.

steps.label: Step 5 — The kill criterion column
steps.body: 'If auto-approval rate on the cohort is below 40% by 21 September 2026, sunset the pilot. Do not extend.' Cohort, threshold, action, date.

steps.label: Step 6 — Owner and review
steps.body: 'Rohan owns it. Reviewed 21 September.' Not 'the AI team.' Not 'Q3.' One human, one date.

blocks.prompt: A direct report shows you their hypothesis register. Bet 2's 'kill criterion' column reads: 'If user feedback is poor, we'll reassess.' What is your response?

choices.label: Send it back. 'User feedback is poor' is not a kill criterion; cohort, threshold, action, date are missing.
choices.explain: Correct. A kill criterion that the optimistic-future-version-of-you can wriggle out of is not a kill criterion. The whole point is to bind the future you to the choices the present you can defend.

choices.label: Approve. The team will know what 'poor' means in context.
choices.explain: Predictable failure mode. By the time 'poor' is debated, three months are gone and the discussion is about extending. The vagueness is the trap.

choices.label: Approve and add 'CSAT below 7' as a metric.
choices.explain: Better, but CSAT alone is gameable, lagging, and not cohort-scoped. The full criterion needs cohort + threshold + action + date.

choices.label: Tell them to talk to Legal first.
choices.explain: Wrong department. Legal cannot help the team write a kill criterion; product and engineering can.

hi-IN.title: Bhabhiji ka SIP test
hi-IN.md:
Bhabhiji ne pucha — "yeh AI bet ka matlab kya hai?" Tu samjha — "3 mutual fund SIPs samjho. Har SIP mein 90 din baad NAV check karte hain. Agar NAV target se neeche hai, SIP rok dete hain. Agar achchi return hai, doosri SIP shuru karte hain."

Bhabhiji boli — "toh SIP hi karo na, AI ka tag kyun chahiye?" Bhabhiji jeet gayi. **Wahi baat hai**: AI bet portfolio = SIP for capability shifts, with cleaner kill rules than most fund managers ever write down.

en.title: The same point in fund-manager English
en.md: An AI bet portfolio is a SIP into capability shifts, with kill criteria sharper than most fund managers will commit to in writing. The discipline is not new; only the asset class is.

blocks.md:
A 12-month AI roadmap is fiction. Capability shifts every quarter; vendor pricing shifts every month; your assumptions about user adoption are wrong almost every time. **Commit to a 90-day kill criterion or you have committed to nothing.**

The gate is one meeting at the end of each 90-day window. Pre-committed agenda:

1. Read each bet's kill-criterion line out loud, exactly as it was written 90 days ago.
2. Place the actual cohort metric next to it.
3. Apply the action: deepen, narrow, or sunset. No 'extend by one quarter.' No 'the team is showing momentum.'
4. If a bet survives, set the next 90-day kill criterion before leaving the room.
5. If a bet sunsets, the budget moves to the reserved slot — which now has a name.

The gate works because the rule is *boring*. It is not a debate; it is a checklist. The boredom is the feature. Without the boredom, you are back to the slogan economy.

coach.name: Board-Member Bharat
coach.role: Independent director, ex-CFO, has watched two CEOs argue at a 90-day gate that 'momentum' should override the metric

intro: Aap baith jaaiye. Aaj hum 90-day gate ka simulation karte hain.

Main aapko paanch real-life situations dunga jo aapne *pre-committed* kar diye the. Aap bata sakte ho — yeh **honour the kill** hai, ya **defensible exception** hai, ya **theatre that's pretending to be defensible**?
Naya rule — agar aap 'extend by one quarter' bolte hain bina kuch defensible reason ke, main aapko mute kar dunga.

scenarios.situation: Bet 1 (support draft). Kill criterion: 55% draft acceptance by day 90. At day 90, acceptance is 41%. PM argues: 'team morale is high, we are close.'
scenarios.explain: Honour. 'Team morale' and 'close' are exactly the words the pre-commit was meant to defeat. 41 vs 55 is a 25% gap; that's not 'close', that's a 50% miss when you account for typical optimism bias.

scenarios.situation: Bet 2 (claims pre-fill). Kill criterion: 40% auto-approval. At day 90, auto-approval is 38% but a regulatory clarification arrived on day 87 that fundamentally changes the eligible-claim definition.
scenarios.explain: Defensible exception, but only because the rule changed mid-flight. Document the regulatory change; reset the kill criterion against the new definition; commit to a new 60-day mini-gate. Do not silently extend.

scenarios.situation: Bet 3 (internal copilot). Kill criterion: 8 weekly active users. At day 90, weekly active is 11. PM argues: 'we should expand scope to more teams.'
scenarios.explain: Honour the *deepen* path. The bet passed; that's a kill criterion working in the positive direction. Deepen with a fresh 90-day criterion — say 25 WAU by day 180 — before scope creep eats the win.

scenarios.situation: Bet at day 90: kill criterion was 'CSAT > 7.5'. Actual: 7.4. PM argues: 'within margin of error, statistically not different from 7.5.'
scenarios.explain: Theatre. Statistical-sigificance arguments at the gate are almost always retroactive. Either the kill criterion should have been written with confidence intervals to start with, or 7.4 means 7.4. Honour the kill; the lesson is for the next register.

scenarios.situation: Bet at day 90: kill criterion missed by 18%. PM produces a slide showing 'a new model release next month will change everything.'
scenarios.explain: Theatre. 'Next month's model' is the most-used pivot in the AI playbook and the least-correlated with day-180 outcomes. Sunset the bet; let the new model be the trigger to *reopen* the question, not the excuse to keep the current bet alive.

scenarios.situation: Bet at day 90: kill criterion of 40% met at exactly 40.1%. PM asks: 'do we deepen?'
scenarios.explain: Defensible — the rule says deepen — but the margin is so tight that the right deepen action is *narrow* deepen: same cohort, double the volume, fresh 60-day criterion. Don't deepen-and-expand on a barely-passing signal.

blocks.title: The classic trap: all-in on one flagship feature
blocks.md:
If your AI program has exactly one flagship and your year is built around its launch, you have not built a portfolio; you have built a single point of failure with a budget. The flagship trap survives because it is *legible* — easier to explain to a board, easier to celebrate at all-hands, easier to put on a deck.

It is also where 87% of AI budgets evaporate. The rule of thumb that earns the right to live: **no AI bet over 50% of program budget, ever.** If a single bet wants more than half, split it into a phase-gated sequence of smaller bets first.

blocks.prompt: You're at the 90-day gate. Order the steps in the meeting, exactly as they should happen.

items.label: Read each bet's pre-committed kill criterion out loud, verbatim.
items.detail: Reading aloud is not theatre; it forces the room to remember what was promised, before the new arguments start.

items.label: Place the actual cohort metric next to the criterion.
items.detail: On a single line. Visible to everyone. No interpretation yet.

items.label: Apply the action — deepen, narrow, or sunset — by the rule.
items.detail: If the criterion was met: deepen. If close: narrow. If missed: sunset.

items.label: Set the next 90-day criterion for surviving bets.
items.detail: Before leaving the room. Otherwise, drift sets in.

items.label: Reallocate sunset budget to the reserved slot.
items.detail: The reserved slot may now get its first name. This is when you earn it.

items.label: Update the hypothesis register and circulate it within 24 hours.
items.detail: The register is the artefact; the meeting is the rehearsal. Circulating it makes the decisions sticky.

blocks.hint: Read the rule before the metric. The order protects you from your own optimism.

blocks.instruction: Write the kill-criterion line for one AI bet at your company, in 25 words or fewer. It must contain: a cohort, a threshold, an action verb (deepen / narrow / sunset), and a date. If you cannot fit all four, the bet is not yet a bet — say so.
blocks.expected:
Strong example:

'For the support-draft bet on English-only tier-1 tickets, if agent draft-acceptance is below 55% on day 90 (14 September 2026), sunset and reallocate budget.'

Note what's in it: cohort (English-only tier-1), threshold (55%), action (sunset), date (14 Sep). 26 words is acceptable; 47 words means you over-hedged.

Weak pattern: 'If the AI tool is not adding value to the team, we will reconsider.' (No cohort, no threshold, no action, no date. Theatre.)

blocks.prompt: Which of the following are signs your portfolio is at risk of becoming a one-bet program in disguise? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: One bet has grown to 64% of total budget after a mid-year reallocation.
choices.explain: Yes. Mid-year creep past 50% on a single bet is the canonical 'flagship in disguise' signature. Forces a portfolio decision back into the room.

choices.label: Three bets each have signed-off, written kill criteria with cohort and date.
choices.explain: Opposite. This is exactly what a healthy 3-bet portfolio looks like.

choices.label: Two bets share the same engineering team and the same backend platform with no isolation.
choices.explain: Yes. Operational coupling means 'one bet' in disguise — failure or delay on the platform takes both bets down. Independence is what made them three.

choices.label: The reserved slot has been left unfilled at the day-90 gate.
choices.explain: Not necessarily a problem. The reserved slot is supposed to be unfilled until you earn the right to name it. Filling it prematurely is the failure mode here, not leaving it empty.

hi-IN.title: Three SIPs vs one FD — same logic, different asset class
hi-IN.md:
Mummy ne kabhi ek hi mutual fund mein paise nahi rakhe. Hamesha 3 SIPs — large-cap, mid-cap, ek tax-saver. Logic — "agar ek girta hai, doosre cover kar lete hain."

Aur tu yahan ₹2.4 crore ek 'flagship feature' mein daal raha hai? Mummy ko mat dikhana yeh deck. Mummy ka mind sound hai. Tera nahi.

en.title: Your mother's portfolio logic
en.md: Your mother never put her savings in a single mutual fund. She runs three concurrent SIPs across categories. The argument she would not make for her own retirement is the argument you are making for ₹2.4 crore of company budget on a single AI flagship. She would notice. So would your CFO if you spelled it out the same way.

blocks.title: Field Notes: ₹14 cr on one bet
blocks.source: Anonymous CFO at a Series-C Indian fintech
blocks.story:
Our CEO wanted a moonshot. ₹14 crore — entire AI budget — on one bet: an autonomous customer-support agent. Six months of work. No fallback bets. No staged kill criteria.

Month 9: agent live with 8% of tickets. Quality scores below the human team. Monthly burn ₹40L. CEO doubled down: 'just give it more data.' Month 12: still 9%, quality still down. **Agent shelved.** ₹14 cr written off. AI team morale: gone. Two principal engineers left.

What would have changed it: the same ₹14 cr split into 3 bets (₹6cr / ₹5cr / ₹3cr), each with a 90-day kill criterion. Even if the moonshot still failed, the other two would have produced something shippable AND a culture that survives kills. Single-bet portfolios are a culture risk, not just a financial risk.
blocks.takeaway: Single-bet AI portfolios concentrate risk; staged kill criteria across 3 bets distribute both the loss and the learning.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: 3 bets, ₹3.6 cr
blocks.setup: Vikrant has ₹3.6 crore for AI in Q1 2026. His engineering team is excited about an autonomous agent moonshot. His CFO wants the safe bet (RAG over docs). The board wants 'transformative.' All three want everything to be the One Big Bet.

coach.name: Ex-CTO-now-advisor Ananth
coach.role: Built, sold, and unwound 4 AI products at scale

stages.prompt: Should Vikrant put all ₹3.6 cr on the moonshot?

options.label: Yes — engineering loves it, board wants 'transformative,' send it.
options.explain: Single-bet portfolio. If moonshot fails (and most do), nothing else lands. Culture and capital both burned.

options.label: Split into 3: ₹1.8cr safe (RAG over docs), ₹1.2cr stretch (workflow agent), ₹0.6cr moonshot.
options.explain: Right. Tiered exposure. 60/33/16 split lets the moonshot fail without taking the safer wins down.

options.label: All-safe: ₹3.6cr on the RAG bet. No moonshot at all.
options.explain: Over-conservative. Diversification works in both directions; you also need at least one stretch bet.

stages.prompt: Day 45 of the moonshot bet. It's missing every milestone by 30%+. CEO says 'give it more time.' Vikrant's move?

options.label: Honor the pre-committed kill criterion. Stop. Write the post-mortem. Reallocate the engineers.
options.explain: The kill criterion was the discipline. Honoring it preserves trust for ALL future bets, not just this one.

options.label: Extend by 30 days to give CEO breathing room.
options.explain: Soft kill criterion = no kill criterion. Every future bet's discipline now leaks.

options.label: Quietly let it run while telling CEO it's still on track.
options.explain: Trust-destroying. CEO will find out at month 6 and the trust loss is worse than the kill.

stages.prompt: Day 90: bet 1 hits its outcome (CAC -8%), bet 2 partially hits (mixed signal), moonshot killed at day 45. What does Vikrant report to the board?

options.label: All three honestly. The win, the partial, and the kill — with the post-mortem from the kill.
options.explain: Honest portfolio reporting builds board trust. The kill is a feature; the board sees discipline.

options.label: Just the win. Soft-pedal the kill.
options.explain: Boards always find out. Soft-pedaling once destroys credibility for the next portfolio.

options.label: Frame the kill as 'pivot' to make it sound positive.
options.explain: Euphemism is read as evasion. 'Killed at day 45 per pre-committed criterion' lands far better.

outcomes.perfect: S-tier. Vikrant ships a 1-win, 1-partial, 1-kill quarter. The board approves Q2 portfolio at ₹4.2 cr because the kill criterion proved discipline. Engineering culture intact.
outcomes.good: Solid. Portfolio held its discipline. Bet 2's partial signal needs another quarter to call.
outcomes.learn: Re-read the kill-criterion section. The criterion has no value if it's negotiable.

points: Concentration is worse than diversification for AI bets; binary 90-day outcomes punish single-bet programs.
The 3-bet portfolio with one reserved slot is the only structure that buys you a second cycle.
The hypothesis register is one page; empty cells are visible debt; the page is the program.
A 90-day kill criterion missed by 25% is missed; 'momentum' and 'next month's model' are the two phrases that should make you suspicious.
If a bet exceeds 50% of total program budget, you have a flagship in disguise; split it before the gate, not after.

blocks.prompt: Look at your current AI program (or a peer's, if you don't run one). Name three bets and the reserved slot. For each named bet, write the one-line kill criterion. The first time you do this, at least one bet will not have a defensible criterion. Note which one and why — that's the bet most at risk of becoming theatre.

lessons.title: Team Topologies for AI
lessons.subtitle: AI cell or AI factory? Pick the wrong one and the program dies in queue

audioChapters.label: Opening — the AI council that became a queue
Mental model: AI cell vs AI factory

blocks.md:
Six months in, your AI program has 14 ideas, 3 ships, and a 17-week backlog at the central AI team. Product managers have stopped bringing new ideas. The Slack channel that used to have 40 messages a day has 4. The program is not dead; it is centralised, and centralisation has become the disease.

This lesson is about choosing the structure that lets the program survive month 6. By the end you will be able to tell, in one diagnostic conversation, whether your company should run an AI cell or an AI factory, where the governance layer fits, and the single sentence to ask any team that has built three demos and shipped none.

blocks.title: Mental model: AI cell vs AI factory
blocks.md:
Two clean patterns; everything in between is debt.

**AI cell** is a small team — usually 2 to 6 people — embedded inside an existing product team. They share the team's roadmap. They ship features end-to-end. The 'why' lives in the product team, not in the AI cell. Best when you do not yet know which problems will be load-bearing.

**AI factory** is a horizontal platform — usually 15+ people — that owns shared capability (models, eval harness, LLM gateway, red-team set, cost monitoring, kill switch) and serves multiple product teams above it. Product teams own the 'why'; the factory owns the 'how'. Best when you have stable product surfaces, regulatory load, and roughly four or more concurrent AI features.

The rule of thumb: **start as a cell, graduate to a factory when at least three concurrent product teams need the same capability and the cell becomes a bottleneck.** Centralising before that is org-chart theatre; staying decentralised after that is duplicated work and missed audits.

blocks.caption: Watch a cell become two cells become a factory as concurrent demand crosses the threshold.

hi-IN.title: AI Council ne queue ban diya
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, scene yeh hai. Series-C SaaS, 200 engineers. CEO ne kaha — "hum AI mein serious hain, council banao." Council bana — 7 log, hafte mein ek meeting, har AI launch ko approve karna padta hai. **3 mahine baad** backlog 17 hafte ka. Product teams ne AI features socheneka chod diya — "council mein 4 mahine lagenge, bhul jao."

6 mahine baad CEO ne pucha — "AI velocity gir kyun gayi?" Council ne presentation banayi — 14 slides — explaining why velocity is hard. Council apne aap ka project ban gayi. **Centralise too early, queue ban jaata hai. Decentralise too late, har team apna red-team likh raha hota hai.**

en.title: When the council becomes the queue
en.md: A 200-engineer SaaS spun up an 'AI Council' early. Within three months, the council was a 17-week queue and product teams had stopped bringing AI ideas. Six months later the council produced a 14-slide deck explaining why velocity was hard. The pattern is universal: centralise before the demand exists and the council becomes its own project.

blocks.md:
If you build an AI factory, you also build a governance layer. The mistake is building it thick. A thick layer is a council with monthly meetings, a slide-deck review process, and a 14-page policy doc. A thin layer is one page of rules, one named owner, three things that always block release, and one kill switch.

A thin governance layer fits on a single page. It says, in order:

1. **What gets evaluated** (eval set name, version, threshold).
2. **What blocks release** (failure rate, missing red-team report, no named owner, no kill switch).
3. **Who can override** (one human, named).
4. **What gets logged on every AI inference** (cost, latency, failure flag, user ID, prompt category).
5. **The kill switch** (who can pull it, in how many minutes, with what fallback).

A crisp number from a 2026 Bengaluru fintech audit: thin governance (one page, signed by the CTO) cleared 11 production AI features through the regulator's review in 9 weeks. The peer company with 47 pages of policy and a council was still on feature 2 at the same date.

blocks.title: Translation moment — 'we need AI ethics' becomes a thin governance page

steps.label: Step 1 — The English question
steps.body: Board director: 'We need an AI ethics policy.' True. But 'AI ethics policy' decays into 47 pages and zero blocked launches without translation.

steps.label: Step 2 — Pick what the policy actually blocks
steps.body: Translate to: 'What concrete things should never reach a user?' Answer: model that fails > X% on the eval set, no red-team report, no named owner, no kill switch, no per-inference logging. Five things.

steps.label: Step 3 — Pick the eval set
steps.body: Name it: 'fintech-eval-v3, 1,200 prompts, last red-teamed 18 March 2026.' If the eval set does not exist, that is the first thing to build, not the policy doc.

steps.label: Step 4 — Pick the override
steps.body: One named human can override the threshold (e.g. CTO). The override produces a written log entry, automatically. No committee, no slide deck. Override is rare; record-keeping is mandatory.

steps.label: Step 5 — Sign the page
steps.body: CTO signs. CISO signs. Date stamped. Lives in version control. The 47-page policy doc, if it ever existed, is now an appendix that no one reads, and that is fine.

blocks.prompt: An 'AI ethics policy doc' that runs to 47 pages and has been approved by Legal. What is its leadership-grade weakness?

choices.label: It does not specify what concretely blocks a release; therefore in practice nothing is blocked.
choices.explain: Correct. A policy that does not name the concrete artefact (eval set, threshold, owner, kill switch) cannot be enforced; it only generates audit trails of compliance theatre.

choices.label: It is too long for engineers to read.
choices.explain: Symptom, not cause. Engineers will read 47 pages once if it changes their behaviour; they will skip 4 pages forever if it does not.

choices.label: Legal approval is not the same as engineering approval.
choices.explain: True but tangential. The deeper problem is the absence of testable gates regardless of who signed.

choices.label: It will need to be updated quarterly.
choices.explain: Operational concern, not the structural one. A 1-page thin policy needs updating too, and that is fine.

hi-IN.title: Compliance vs Karavarat — Indian governance ka real test
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, ek RBI inspection mein ek bank ne 480 page ka AI policy doc dikhaya. Inspector ne pucha — "is policy ne kabhi kuch block kiya hai?" Bank ne kaha — "haan, hum bahut serious hain." Inspector ne pucha — "specific example?" Bank ka silence. Inspector ne report mein likha — *"governance documentation extensive but functionally inert."*

Agli company ne 1 page dikhaya — "yeh hamari eval threshold hai, yeh kill switch hai, yeh override karne wala banda hai." Inspector khush. Audit pass.

**Inspector log nahi padhte. Inspector activity dekhte hain.** Tera 47-page policy nahi, tera last *block* matter karta hai.

en.title: What a regulator actually checks
en.md: A regulator does not measure your policy by its weight; they measure it by its last enforced action. 'Show me the most recent release this policy blocked.' If the answer is 'we have not had to', the policy is inert. Regulators have stopped finding 480 pages reassuring.

blocks.text: Move 2 — The 'where does the why live?' question

blocks.md:
When you walk into a struggling AI program, ask one question:

> *"Who, outside this AI team, can articulate the user problem this team is solving in one sentence, without me prompting?"*

If the answer is 'no one' — the program is rudderless. The 'why' lives only in the AI team's slide deck, and slide decks are not strategy. This is the failure mode of demo-only teams.

If the answer is 'three product managers and one customer success lead can each say it, in roughly the same words' — the program has roots. The 'why' lives in the company, not in the AI team. The team can be replaced; the 'why' will pull in a new team.

The diagnostic is brutal because it is hard to fake. You cannot prep three people for the question without rehearsing them, and rehearsal is visible. A crisp number from a 2026 Pune SaaS rebuild: of the 8 AI initiatives that survived their second year, 7 had three or more non-AI-team employees who could articulate the user problem. Of the 14 that did not, 13 could not produce a single such sentence.

coach.name: Board-Member Bharat
coach.role: Independent director, has personally diagnosed two struggling AI programs by talking to non-AI staff for 20 minutes

intro: Aap aaye. Aaj scenarios hain — aapko team topology decide karni hai: **AI cell**, **AI factory**, ya **none yet** (matlab abhi structure ki zaroorat hi nahi).

Yaad rakhiye — wrong structure ka cost ek saal hota hai. Centralise too early, queue. Decentralise too late, duplication. Sahi answer 'depends' ho sakta hai, lekin **kis pe depend karta hai** — woh aapko bolna hai.

scenarios.situation: 12-person early-stage startup, one product, 1 CEO + 1 CTO + 8 engs + 2 designers. Wants to add AI co-pilot to product. Currently: nothing.
scenarios.explain: No structure yet. At 12 people, naming an 'AI cell' is over-engineering. Two engs experiment inside the existing product team and ship. Structure becomes meaningful around 30-50 people, not 12.

scenarios.situation: 200-engineer Series-C SaaS, 6 product lines, 2 of them starting to play with LLM features independently. No shared eval, no shared gateway, no governance. Each team has rolled its own.
scenarios.explain: Factory time. Two product lines duplicating work and a third about to start is the canonical 'graduate to factory' signal. Build a thin platform: gateway, eval harness, kill switch. Don't build a council.

scenarios.situation: 60-engineer Series-B fintech with one main product. Wants to add AI to one specific user surface (claims). No prior AI work; no shared infra.
scenarios.explain: Cell. Embed 2 ML engineers and a PM inside the existing claims team. End-to-end ownership. Don't build factory infrastructure for a single bet; you would be supplying capacity that has no demand.

scenarios.situation: 1,200-engineer enterprise insurance, 4 product lines, regulatory load is heavy (IRDAI), 3 product lines already have AI features in production with separate eval pipelines and no shared logging.
scenarios.explain: Factory, urgently. With this regulatory exposure and three concurrent eval pipelines, an audit will surface inconsistencies you cannot defend. Build a thin factory in 90 days; do not wait for the next IRDAI review to force the issue.

scenarios.situation: 85-engineer D2C company. CEO wants 'an AI strategy.' No specific user problem named; no team has yet asked for AI tooling.
scenarios.explain: No structure yet. The CEO has not done the strategy work; no team is asking for the structure. Building a cell or factory here would be solving for the deck, not for any actual user. Push back: ask which curve shifted, which problem you are attacking.

scenarios.situation: 300-engineer health-tech, 4 product lines, 2 already shipped LLM features, 1 in active build. Eval is per-team but partially shared via informal Slack channels. Compliance officer is asking for centralised audit trail.
scenarios.explain: Factory. Compliance officer asking for audit trail is the trigger. Health-tech regulatory surface plus three concurrent product lines with informal coordination is exactly where factory pays back fastest.

blocks.title: The classic trap: centralise too early or decentralise too late
blocks.md:
Both directions kill programs. Centralising before three concurrent product teams need the same capability turns the central team into a queue, and product teams stop bringing ideas. Decentralising past four concurrent product teams produces duplicated eval pipelines, inconsistent kill switches, and an audit that takes 14 weeks to reconstruct.

The trap exists because the *right* timing is hard to see from the inside. The diagnostic — 'how many concurrent product teams are building AI features today?' — is the cheapest way to know. **Three is the threshold.** Below three, run cells. At three, start the factory. Above four, the factory had better already exist.

blocks.prompt: You're scoping a new AI factory. Order the things you build, in priority order.

items.label: The shared eval harness with versioned test sets.
items.detail: Without an eval harness, every team cargo-cults their own. The harness is the cheapest, highest-leverage factory artefact.

items.label: The LLM gateway with per-team rate limits, logging, and cost monitoring.
items.detail: Logging on every inference is non-negotiable. You cannot diagnose what you do not log.

items.label: The thin governance page (eval threshold, owner, kill switch, override rule).
items.detail: Single page. Signed by CTO. In version control. Block release on the page, not on a council.

items.label: The kill switch for any AI feature, with a named on-call rota.
items.detail: Maximum time-to-disable: 15 minutes. Fallback path: defined in writing for each feature.

items.label: The shared red-team prompt library.
items.detail: Adversarial prompts are too expensive to redo per team. Centralise once; let teams add team-specific extensions.

items.label: The internal documentation site listing all AI features, owners, eval results, and kill switches.
items.detail: Discoverability. If a regulator asks 'what AI is in production today?' the answer should be one URL, not three weeks of meetings.

blocks.hint: Eval first; it makes everything else honest. Documentation site is necessary but should ride on top of the others.

blocks.instruction: Walk through your company's current AI footprint. Count concurrent product teams that are building AI features today. Below three: confirm you should be running cells (or nothing). At three: scope a 90-day plan to stand up a thin factory. Above four with no factory: name one thing that an audit would surface as inconsistent across teams. Write your one-line diagnosis.
blocks.expected:
Strong example:

'Currently 4 product teams are shipping LLM features with no shared eval harness; an audit would surface 4 different prompt-handling approaches and 0 consistent failure-rate measurements. Verdict: factory is overdue; first artefact to build is shared eval, signed off in 60 days, owner = staff ML engineer Anika.'

Weak pattern: 'We have AI happening across the company.' (Vague; cannot drive a decision. The point of the exercise is to count and name.)

blocks.prompt: Which of the following are reliable signs your AI team is demo-only, not user-facing? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: No one outside the AI team can articulate, in one sentence, the user problem the team is solving.
choices.explain: Yes. The 'where does the why live' diagnostic. If the why lives only in the AI team's deck, you have a demo team.

choices.label: The AI team owns the LLM gateway and eval harness.
choices.explain: Healthy factory pattern. Owning shared capability is what factories do; not a sign of a demo team.

choices.label: The team's last 6 months produced 14 demos and 0 features in production.
choices.explain: Yes. Demo-to-ship ratio of zero is the unambiguous signature. Sometimes it's because the demos were not connected to a kill criterion; sometimes because no PM owned the surface; the symptom is the same.

choices.label: The team holds a weekly demo session for the rest of the company.
choices.explain: Demos *as a ritual* are fine; it's the demo-to-ship ratio that matters. Weekly demos with monthly ships is a healthy cadence.

hi-IN.title: Joint family vs apartment — same logic
hi-IN.md:
Joint family mein har bhabhi apna kitchen chalati hai? Nahi. Ek kitchen, ek menu, ek sasur jo budget approve karta hai. Aur har bhabhi apne dish ke liye request daalti hai. Wahi factory hai.

Apartment mein har family ka apna kitchen hai. Kyun? Kyunki har family alag hai, alag dietary needs, alag time. Wahi cell hai.

**Joint family chalti hai jab volume zyada hai aur consistency chahiye.** Apartment chalta hai jab har family ka context unique hai. Tera company kaunsa hai? Ye decide kar le, phir structure pick kar.

en.title: Joint family vs apartment block
en.md: A joint family runs one kitchen because the volume is high and consistency matters. An apartment block has one kitchen per family because each context is unique. Your AI org is one of these. Pick which, then build for it.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 7 RAG implementations, 7 security audits
blocks.source: Anonymous CISO at a 600-person Indian SaaS
blocks.story:
Decentralization went too far. Seven product teams each shipped their own RAG implementation between Jan and June 2025. Seven different vector DBs. Seven different chunking strategies. Three different prompt-injection mitigations (one team had none).

My team had 7 attack surfaces to audit. We caught a P0 in team #4's setup — a customer's PII was being logged in plaintext to a vendor we hadn't approved. **₹47 lakh remediation. 6 weeks of rework. Trust with our enterprise clients took a quarter to repair.**

We centralized after that incident. Built a shared RAG platform with one approved vector DB, one chunking library, one prompt sanitizer. Took 4 months to migrate all 7 teams. Team velocity dropped 14% during migration. Worth every percent — we now sleep at night.
blocks.takeaway: Decentralize first; centralize the moment 3+ teams duplicate the same surface. Earlier is bureaucracy; later is breach.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: AI Cell or AI Factory?
blocks.setup: Vikrant has 8 product teams, each piloting AI. Two have already shipped to customers. Three are mid-build. Three haven't started. CFO wants efficiency. Engineering wants autonomy. Vikrant has 6 weeks to decide org structure.

coach.name: Ex-CTO-now-advisor Ananth
coach.role: Built, sold, and unwound 4 AI products at scale

options.label: Decentralized — each team building their own. Right for early experimentation.
options.explain: Right. With 2 in production and 3 mid-build, decentralized was the correct first move. The question now is when to centralize.

options.label: Already centralized — they all use the same model API.
options.explain: Same API ≠ same architecture. Each team built their own infra around that API. That's the duplication risk.

options.label: Chaos — should have been centralized from day 1.
options.explain: Day-1 centralization usually ships nothing for 6 months. Decentralized first IS the right pattern.

stages.prompt: When should Vikrant centralize the AI infra?

options.label: When 3+ teams are duplicating the same surface (RAG, prompt eval, model gateway). Now might be right.
options.explain: Right trigger. Duplication ≥ 3 teams = centralize that surface. Let unique team work stay decentralized.

options.label: Centralize everything immediately to maximize efficiency.
options.explain: Premature centralization. Unique team work shouldn't be centralized just because some surfaces should be.

options.label: Never centralize; teams know best.
options.explain: Becomes the 7-RAG security incident.

options.label: Centralize at the next reorg cycle, regardless of state.
options.explain: Calendar-driven centralization is bureaucratic. Trigger-driven (3+ teams duplicating) is right.

stages.prompt: Vikrant's design: a small AI Platform team (3 engineers) builds shared RAG + prompt eval + model gateway. Product teams keep their unique work. What's missing?

options.label: A governance layer — who decides what graduates from a team into the platform.
options.explain: Right. Without governance, the platform team becomes a shadow PMO. Decision rights matter more than architecture.

options.label: Nothing. The 3-engineer platform team is enough.
options.explain: Misses governance. Architecture without decision rights creates bottlenecks.

options.label: More engineers. Make platform team 8 strong.
options.explain: Over-staffing the platform team is a common over-correction. 3 is right; governance is what's missing.

outcomes.perfect: S-tier. Vikrant lands a hybrid org with explicit governance. 6 months later, 3 product teams ship faster on shared infra; the unique work stays decentralized. CISO sleeps.
outcomes.good: Solid. Architecture is right; governance layer needs another iteration.
outcomes.learn: Re-read the trigger section. The 'when' of centralization matters more than the 'whether'.

points: AI cell and AI factory are the only two clean structures; everything in between is debt.
Start as a cell; graduate to a factory when at least three concurrent product teams need the same capability.
Thin governance is a single page that blocks releases; thick policy is 47 pages that block nothing.
Where the 'why' lives tells you whether the program will survive a leadership change. Three external articulators, minimum.
Centralise too early and the council becomes a queue; decentralise too late and the audit becomes a scavenger hunt.

blocks.prompt: Walk to the desk of one product manager, customer success lead, or support manager outside your AI team. Ask them, in one sentence, what user problem your AI work is solving. Listen carefully. If they pause for more than a few seconds, your 'why' has not taken root; that is your first job before any new bet.

lessons.title: Governance Without Theatre
lessons.subtitle: Real eval gates beat policy docs every audit, every quarter

audioChapters.label: Opening — the policy doc that blocked nothing
Mental model: real eval gates beat policy docs

blocks.md:
Your Compliance head walks in with a 47-page AI ethics policy. Legal has signed off. The CEO wants you to circulate it. Six months later, an AI feature ships with a 4% hallucination rate on financial answers, no one is named to disable it, and the customer who lost ₹38,000 is talking to a journalist. You ask Compliance which line of the policy was supposed to prevent this. They cannot point to one.

This is governance theatre. The policy was a document, not a control. By the end of this lesson, you will know the difference between a real eval gate and a policy doc, what a kill switch actually looks like in production, and the single page of artefacts you must write down before any AI feature touches money, identity, or health.

blocks.title: Mental model: real eval gates beat policy docs, every time
blocks.md:
A **policy doc** describes what the company aspires to. It contains nouns: 'fairness', 'accountability', 'transparency.' It can be 47 pages long and approved by Legal. It blocks nothing.

An **eval gate** is a number with a threshold and a name. 'Failure rate on the financial-advice eval set v3 must be below 1.5% before any user is exposed.' It is two sentences long. It blocks releases.

The difference is testability. A policy doc cannot fail; an eval gate can. **Anything that cannot fail cannot govern.** That is the entire idea, and it took the field five years to admit it.

The leader's job is not to make the policy doc better. The leader's job is to convert every line of the policy doc into either an eval gate, a logging requirement, a kill switch, or a named-owner artefact. If a line cannot be converted, delete it. The 47-page doc collapses to one page. That is governance.

blocks.caption: An eval gate in motion. Watch a release attempt fail at the 1.5% threshold, three times, before the team finds the bug.

hi-IN.title: Compliance officer ka 47 page report
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, ek bank ka compliance officer Pradeep tha. 47-page AI policy doc — har Tuesday review meeting — har Friday newsletter. Six months baad ek incident ho gaya — chatbot ne customer ko galat tax advice de di. Loss ₹4.2 lakh.

Pradeep ne policy ka section 14.3 dikhaya — "AI must align with regulatory guidance." Customer bola — "toh kya hua, paisa kahan hai?" Pradeep ne kaha — "hum compliant the."

Problem yeh hai — Pradeep technically sahi tha. Policy mein likha tha — "must align." Lekin policy ne kabhi check nahi kiya. Eval gate hota toh chatbot launch hi nahi hota. **Compliant honaa aur safe honaa do alag cheezein hain.**

en.title: Compliant is not the same as safe
en.md: A bank's chatbot gave a customer wrong tax advice. The compliance officer pointed to section 14.3 of the AI policy: 'AI must align with regulatory guidance.' Technically he was right; the policy did say so. But the policy did not check. An eval gate would have failed the launch. Compliant and safe are different controls; the field has begun to admit they were conflating them.

blocks.md:
A kill switch is the smallest, cheapest, highest-leverage piece of AI governance you can build. The complete spec fits in three lines:

1. **Who can pull it.** A named role, on a 24/7 rota. Not 'the AI team.' One human at a time.
2. **In how many minutes.** A maximum time from decision to feature-disabled. The industry default is 15 minutes; tougher surfaces (money, health) should be 5.
3. **What the user sees instead.** A defined fallback path. Plain old form. Human agent. Cached previous answer. Anything but a generic error.

That's it. If you cannot answer all three for every AI feature in production, you do not have a kill switch; you have an aspiration.

A crisp number from a 2026 Mumbai banking incident: a chatbot quoting wrong interest rates was disabled in 8 minutes by an on-call SRE because the kill switch was wired and the rota was clear. The next-door bank with the same vendor and no kill switch took 9 hours and lost ₹2.7 crore in misquotes.

blocks.title: Translation moment — 'we should be able to turn it off' becomes a kill switch spec

steps.label: Step 1 — The English question
steps.body: CEO in a postmortem: 'We should be able to turn it off.' Everyone nods. Nothing changes.

steps.label: Step 2 — Pick the named on-call
steps.body: Translate to: 'Priya, Anika, Rohan rotate weekly. PagerDuty escalation. Backup: head of platform.' If you cannot name three humans, you have a one-person dependency.

steps.label: Step 3 — Pick the time-to-disable
steps.body: '15 minutes from page to feature-flag-off.' This forces engineering to wire a feature flag to a single button — not a deploy, not a config push, a flag.

steps.label: Step 4 — Pick the fallback
steps.body: 'Form-based claim entry; estimated processing time 24 hrs; show banner explaining the AI flow is paused.' If the fallback is 'show error', users will assume the company is broken.

steps.label: Step 5 — Run a fire drill
steps.body: Quarterly. The on-call pulls the switch on a low-traffic feature, you measure time-to-disable. If you have never run a drill, you do not have a kill switch; you have a screenshot of one.

blocks.prompt: Your kill-switch design says: 'The AI team can disable any feature within 30 minutes by reaching out to the on-call platform engineer.' What is wrong with it?

choices.label: It uses 'the AI team' (not a named human), 30 minutes is too long for production AI, and 'reaching out' is not a defined channel.
choices.explain: Correct. Three failure modes in one sentence. A real spec names a person, has a target under 15 minutes, and uses a single defined trigger (a button or a CLI command, not a Slack message).

choices.label: It does not name the regulator who would be informed.
choices.explain: Tangential. Regulator notification is a separate workflow; it follows the kill action, it does not gate it.

choices.label: 30 minutes is fine for most surfaces.
choices.explain: False. 30 minutes is unsafe for any user-facing AI on money, identity, or health. It is acceptable only for internal-tooling features.

choices.label: Nothing; it is reasonable.
choices.explain: It is exactly the kind of language that sounds reasonable in a deck and falls apart in production.

hi-IN.title: Bijli ka switch vs Bijli ka MCB
hi-IN.md:
Tera ghar mein **bedroom ka switch** hai — fan band karta hai. **MCB** main panel pe hai — pure ghar ki bijli kaat sakta hai. Tu kabhi MCB ke baare mein nahi sochta jab tak kuch jaldi ka emergency nahi ho.

AI mein, feature-flag is the bedroom switch. Kill switch is the MCB. **MCB ke bina, jab fire lagta hai, tu ek ek room jaake fan band karta phirega.** 9 ghante mein incident handle hota hai. MCB hota toh 8 minute mein. Yeh choice hai — pehle hi MCB lagao, ya post-mortem mein cry karo.

en.title: Feature flag vs main breaker
en.md: A feature flag is the bedroom light switch. A kill switch is the main breaker. You don't think about the main breaker until something is on fire, at which point you really, really wish you knew where it was. The same logic applies to AI in production.

blocks.md:
There are exactly four artefacts that must be written down before any AI feature touches money, identity, or health. Anything more is bureaucracy; anything less is theatre.

1. **The eval card.** Eval set name, version, threshold, last red-team date, last failure-rate measurement. One page.
2. **The kill switch spec.** Owner rota, time-to-disable, fallback path. Three lines.
3. **The logging schema.** What is logged on every AI inference: cost, latency, failure flag, user category, prompt category. Schema, not prose.
4. **The named owner.** One human, with email, with a manager named for escalation. Not 'team.' Not 'rotates monthly.' One human at a time, named, dated.

These four artefacts together fit on roughly four pages. They are version-controlled. They are signed by the CTO and the CISO. They survive an audit because they describe what was done, not what was planned. The 47-page policy doc, if your company writes one, is now an appendix; it does not gate releases.

A crisp number from a 2026 IRDAI inspection of a Pune health-tech: producing the four artefacts on three production AI features took 14 minutes; producing the equivalent narrative from the 47-page policy took 11 days and was still incomplete. Auditors notice.

coach.name: Board-Member Bharat
coach.role: Independent director, has personally reviewed two regulator audits where governance theatre cost the company a public reprimand

intro: Aap aaye. Aaj ka topic — yeh artefact **real governance** hai, ya **theatre** hai, ya **somewhere in between**?
Yaad rakhiye — regulator log nahi padhte, regulator activity dekhte hain. Lawyer nahi check karta jab tak court mein nahi jaate. Customer ek bar bhi nahi padhta.
Toh chaliye — aapka governance kya hai, dekhte hain.

scenarios.situation: An 'AI Council' that meets weekly, reviews slide decks of upcoming AI features, and signs them off. No eval threshold, no kill switch spec, no logging schema. The council has approved 14 features in six months.
scenarios.explain: Theatre. Council approval without eval, kill switch, or logging is a rubber stamp wearing a suit. The 14 approvals look impressive; they are 14 pieces of evidence the council does not block anything.

scenarios.situation: A signed eval card showing failure rate 1.2% on the v3 eval set, last red-teamed 8 weeks ago. Owner named, kill switch wired, logging on. No documented fallback path for the kill switch; assumption is 'the user retries.'
scenarios.explain: Partial. The first three artefacts are real. The fallback path is the gap — 'the user retries' is not a fallback, it is a failure mode. Add a defined fallback (form, human, cached answer) in 14 days; the rest holds.

scenarios.situation: An AI feature ships with: eval threshold (1.5%), red-team report (signed 6 weeks ago), named owner (Anika R), kill switch (Priya rotates, 12-min TTD, human-agent fallback), logging schema (cost / latency / fail / category, signed by CISO).
scenarios.explain: Real governance. All four artefacts present, dated, signed, in version control. This is what auditors believe and what postmortems can reconstruct. Repeat the pattern; do not let it decay.

scenarios.situation: A 47-page AI Ethics Policy approved by Legal in March 2026. Section 14.3 says 'AI must align with regulatory guidance.' No eval set referenced; no kill switch concept; no logging requirement. Policy is reviewed annually.
scenarios.explain: Theatre, in dense form. The policy contains nouns instead of thresholds; the annual review is a calendar event, not a control. Convert each line to an eval, log, kill, or owner artefact, or delete it. The 47 pages will collapse to 4.

scenarios.situation: Eval card present and signed; kill switch wired; logging on. Named owner is 'the AI team.' Manager named for escalation: 'reports to engineering leadership.'
scenarios.explain: Partial. The named-owner artefact is the gap — 'the AI team' is not a named human, and 'engineering leadership' is not an escalation path. Replace both with names within 7 days; the rest holds.

scenarios.situation: Eval card with threshold 1.5%; the eval set has 14 prompts, all written by the AI team itself, no red-team contribution. No external attestation.
scenarios.explain: Theatre wearing eval-card clothing. A 14-prompt eval set written by the team being evaluated is a self-report, not a gate. Real eval is a 500+ prompt set with explicit red-team contributions and external attestation, dated within the last quarter.
