blocks.title: The classic trap: policy doc, no enforcement
blocks.md:
The most common, most expensive failure mode in 2024-26 AI governance: a polished policy document that is approved, circulated, never converted to enforceable artefacts, and never updated until the next incident.

The trap is comfortable. The doc looks like governance. Compliance feels covered. Legal has signed off. The CEO has a paragraph for the board deck. None of these activities, taken together, prevent a single bad release.

The fix is mechanical: every line of the policy must convert to an eval gate, a logging requirement, a kill switch, or a named-owner artefact. **If a line cannot be converted, delete the line.** The 47-page policy collapses to one page. That collapse is the work.

blocks.prompt: You're shipping an AI feature into production tomorrow. Order the gates, in priority order — what blocks ship first.

items.label: Eval failure rate below the published threshold on the agreed test set.
items.detail: First gate. If the model fails its own eval, nothing else matters.

items.label: Red-team report from someone outside the team building the feature, dated within 90 days.
items.detail: External attestation. Internal red-team is fine for non-sensitive surfaces; money / identity / health surfaces require an outside party.

items.label: Kill switch wired, on-call rota named, fallback path defined.
items.detail: If you cannot turn it off, you cannot turn it on. The kill switch precedes the launch button.

items.label: Logging schema deployed and dashboard live before any user is exposed.
items.detail: First user must be loggable. Diagnosis after the fact is impossible without it.

items.label: Named owner with a manager-level escalation path.
items.detail: One human, named, with a name above them. 'Team' does not own anything.

items.label: All four cards (eval / kill / logging / owner) signed by CTO + CISO.
items.detail: Signatures on the cards, in version control. The signature is the audit trail.

blocks.hint: Eval first. Logging before users see it. Signatures last but in writing.

blocks.instruction: Pick one AI feature in your company that is in production today (or is about to ship). Try to produce all four artefacts: eval card, kill switch spec, logging schema, named owner. Be honest — if any artefact does not exist, write 'NOT WRITTEN DOWN' for that one and note what you would need to produce it. The exercise is the diagnostic; the answer reveals where the program is theatre.
blocks.expected:
Strong example:

'Feature: claims pre-fill (live since 12 March 2026).
• Eval card: claims-eval-v2, threshold 92% accuracy, last measured 96.4%, last red-team 14 April 2026 (external — 3rd-party security firm). SIGNED.
• Kill switch: Rohan / Aisha / Sandeep rotate weekly. TTD target 8 min, hard 15 min. Fallback: form-based claim, banner. SIGNED.
• Logging: cost, latency, success-flag, claim-category, user-tier. Dashboard live. CISO signed.
• Owner: Anika R. (head ML), escalation to CTO Vinod. Dated 12 May 2026.'

Weak example:

'Feature: chatbot. We have a policy doc. NOT WRITTEN DOWN: eval threshold, kill switch, logging, owner.' (This is exactly the diagnostic you wanted. The chatbot is a regulator-incident waiting to happen; produce the four artefacts in the next sprint.)

blocks.prompt: Which of the following are real governance artefacts that an auditor would accept? (Pick all that apply.)

choices.label: An eval card showing failure rate 1.2% on a 1,200-prompt test set, last red-teamed 6 weeks ago by an external firm.
choices.explain: Yes. Specific test set, specific number, dated external attestation. This is what auditors are trained to recognise.

choices.label: A 47-page AI Ethics Policy approved by Legal.
choices.explain: Theatre. Policies have not been accepted as governance artefacts since the 2024 wave of regulator guidance shifted toward testable controls.

choices.label: A logging schema with cost, latency, success-flag, and prompt-category fields, signed by the CISO and live in production.
choices.explain: Yes. Logging that is deployed and signed is the artefact regulators look for; it is what reconstructs an incident in 24 hours instead of 14 weeks.

choices.label: A weekly AI Council meeting with attendance recorded.
choices.explain: Theatre, even with attendance recorded. Meetings without testable controls are calendar entries, not governance.

hi-IN.title: Building permit vs structural safety check
hi-IN.md:
Bhai, Mumbai mein building bana rahe ho. Aapke paas **building permit** hai — paper hai, signed hai, BMC ne approve kiya hai. Building gir gayi.

Insurance company ne pucha — "structural safety check kaha hai?" Tu bola — "permit hai na." Insurance ne kaha — "permit aur safety check do alag cheezein hain. Permit BMC ke liye hai. Safety check building ke liye hai."

Wahi hai AI mein — **policy doc BMC ke liye hai, eval gate building ke liye hai.** Dono chahiye. Lekin policy doc akela, building girne par, kuch nahi karta.

en.title: Building permit vs structural inspection
en.md: A building permit proves the city approved the design. A structural inspection proves the building is safe. Both are required; only one of them keeps the building standing. AI policy documents are the permit; eval gates are the inspection. Conflating them is how buildings fall down.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 67-page policy, 4 violations shipped
blocks.source: Anonymous Head of Risk at a regulated Indian fintech
blocks.story:
We wrote a 67-page AI policy in Q4 2024. Reviewed by legal, signed by every department head, framed in the boardroom.

Q1 2025: an AI feature shipped that violated 4 policies — including 'no PII in third-party model context.' Nobody noticed. The policy was a document, not a gate.

Incident discovered during a Q2 audit. ₹2.4 cr remediation. **3 months of paused product launches** while we built the actual gates we should have built first. The policy wasn't useless — it told us *what* to enforce — but it had no teeth.

We now have a 6-page policy AND a CI eval gate that blocks deploys when prompt or output trips any of 14 rules. The 6 pages predict behavior; the 67 pages didn't.
blocks.takeaway: Policy docs without enforcement are theatre. The real governance is the eval gate that blocks deploys.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: governance with teeth
blocks.setup: Vikrant's chief risk officer wants a 47-page AI policy doc to show the regulator. Vikrant's engineering team hates writing them; nobody reads them; the last one gathered dust. The regulator is coming in 8 weeks.

coach.name: CFO-Veteran Vinita
coach.role: 30-year CFO who has seen 12 'governance' efforts work and 47 fail

options.label: Yes — write it long; regulators love thoroughness.
options.explain: Long doc = nobody reads it = nobody enforces it. Regulators have learned this too.

options.label: Write a short doc (6-10 pages) AND a CI eval gate that enforces the rules. The doc is the 'why', the gate is the 'how'.
options.explain: Right balance. Short, readable doc + automated enforcement. The doc tells the regulator what's enforced; the gate proves it.

options.label: Skip the doc; only build the gate.
options.explain: Regulator wants to see the rules. Skip it and you can't show them anything for the rules-as-code.

stages.prompt: Engineering pushes back: 'we don't have time to build eval gates for 14 rules in 8 weeks.' What's the move?

options.label: Pick the top 4 rules by impact. Ship gates for those by week 8. Rest of the rules in the next quarter with a documented timeline.
options.explain: Right. Don't try to gate everything; gate the highest-stakes rules first and document the staged plan.

options.label: Push for all 14 gates; accept the slip.
options.explain: Calendar miss; regulator unhappy. Worse than the staged plan.

options.label: Drop the gates entirely; just write the doc.
options.explain: Back to theatre. The whole point is enforcement.

options.label: Outsource the gates to a vendor.
options.explain: Vendor lock-in for governance is its own risk. Build the critical gates in-house, even if v1 is rough.

stages.prompt: Regulator visit. They ask: 'how do you prevent PII leakage to third-party models?' Vikrant's answer?

options.label: 'Page 14 of our policy,' he says, opening the binder.
options.explain: Standard answer; regulator already heard it 47 times today. Won't differentiate Vikrant's company.

options.label: 'Here's the rule, and here's the CI gate that blocks any deploy where the prompt contains PII patterns. Last 90 days: 14 deploys blocked, 0 false negatives in our audit sample.'
options.explain: S-tier answer. Rule + enforcement + evidence. Regulator stops asking; competitor up next.

options.label: 'We trust our engineers to follow the policy.'
options.explain: Worst answer. Regulator hears 'no actual control'. Audit findings inevitable.

outcomes.perfect: Vikrant walks the regulator through gate-evidence, not policy-text. Audit closes clean. The 6-page doc + 14 gates becomes a sales asset for enterprise customers.
outcomes.good: Solid. Top-4 gates ship; rest planned. Regulator acceptable. Worth completing the next 10 in Q3.
outcomes.learn: Re-read the 'doc is theatre' section. Without enforcement, every page of policy is just words.

points: Real eval gates beat policy docs because they are testable; anything that cannot fail cannot govern.
A kill switch is three lines: who, in how many minutes, with what fallback. If you cannot answer all three, you do not have one.
The four artefacts that gate every sensitive AI feature: eval card, kill switch spec, logging schema, named owner. Four pages, four signatures.
If a line of policy cannot convert to an eval / log / kill / owner artefact, delete it. The doc collapses; the program improves.
Auditors do not measure policy by weight; they measure it by the last enforced action.

blocks.prompt: Walk to your most senior AI feature in production. Try to produce its four artefacts in 14 minutes, from memory or from version control. If you cannot, the gap you found is the highest-priority governance work in the company this week.

lessons.subtitle: Honest timelines, named killcriteria, no 18-month vapor

audioChapters.label: Opening — the board doesn't want vapor

blocks.md: Most VPs lose the board on AI by promising too much. The board doesn't punish honest tradeoffs; it punishes vapor that misses by 18 months. By the end of this lesson you'll know the three sentences a board wants to hear, and the two they never want to hear again.

blocks.title: Mental model: the assumption ledger
blocks.md:
A board ask is a forecast. A forecast without an assumption ledger is a wish. Your job is to write down: *what specifically must be true for this to work, by when will we know, what's the rollback if it doesn't.*

Boards don't punish honest assumption ledgers; they punish surprises.

blocks.caption: Two boardroom slides: the vapor version vs. the dated-commitment version, watched 18 months later.

hi-IN.title: AI-first PowerPoint ka khel
hi-IN.md: Founder ne board mein bola *"hum AI-first hain."* Slide pe 4 ChatGPT screenshots. Investor ne pucha *"specifically kya badla?"* — silence. **AI-first matlab kuch nahi hota agar metric pe nahi dikha.** Vapor ka brand color violet hai.

en.title: Buzzwords, briefly
en.md: Boards have heard 'AI-first' enough times that the phrase now triggers skepticism, not enthusiasm. Replace it with 'we will know by Date Y whether bet X moved metric Z.' Different reaction.

blocks.md:
Every AI bet has four numbers worth declaring up-front:

1. **Investment** — actual rupees and people across 90 days.
2. **Expected outcome** — a specific metric delta, with a date.
3. **Confidence** — your own probability estimate (40%? 70%?).
4. **Cost of being wrong** — what you lose if the bet fails.

A board can debate any of these. They cannot debate vibes.

blocks.title: Translation moment: 'we want to use AI to reduce CAC'

steps.label: 1. Frame the bet
steps.body: Specific outcome with a date. Not 'reduce CAC'; 'reduce paid CAC by ≥10% by Sep 30, with no LTV regression'.

steps.label: 2. Investment line
steps.body: Engineers, PM, money, 90-day window. Concrete.

steps.label: 3. Confidence note
steps.body: Your honest probability. 'We think 50-60%; here's why.'

steps.label: 4. Kill criterion
steps.body: By when, and on what number. 'If at day 45 CAC hasn't moved ≥3%, we kill this and reallocate.'

steps.label: 5. The rollback
steps.body: What happens if it fails. Capital and people freed up; what do they do next.

blocks.prompt: What's the most important sentence in a board AI memo?

choices.label: By Date Y, we will know whether metric Z moved by ≥X%; if not, we kill it.
choices.explain: Correct. A board can govern a dated kill criterion. They cannot govern hope.

choices.label: AI is going to revolutionize everything we do.
choices.explain: This is what every board has heard for 24 months. They want specifics now.

choices.label: Our competitors are all using AI.
choices.explain: FOMO is not a strategy. Boards know this.

choices.label: We've allocated ₹4 crore to AI initiatives.
choices.explain: Numbers without outcomes are budget asks, not strategy.

hi-IN.title: Vichaar samay — the assumption ledger
hi-IN.md: Indian boards mein 'AI strategy' ka literal translation hai *"hum sab kuch karenge, kab pata nahi."* Translate it to: *"yeh number, yeh date, yeh kill criterion."* Ek saans mein bol sako toh better.

en.title: The one-breath test
en.md: If your AI commitment doesn't fit in a one-breath sentence — 'X by Y, killing if Z' — you don't have a commitment. You have an intention.

blocks.md:
Boards trust executives who plan for failure. The rollback narrative — what happens if this bet fails, who absorbs the cost, what gets reallocated — is the single most underrated trust-building move with a board.

Most VPs hide the rollback because they think it signals weakness. It doesn't. *Hiding* it signals weakness. *Pre-committing* to it signals competence.

coach.name: Board-Member Bharat
coach.role: Independent director, 14 board seats over 20 years

intro: Tell me whether each VP is being **honest**, **vague**, or **selling**.
I've sat through 800+ AI memos. Pick carefully.

scenarios.situation: VP says: 'AI will transform our customer support entirely. We expect significant improvements.'
scenarios.explain: Vague. No metric, no date, no kill criterion. Board cannot govern this.

scenarios.situation: VP says: 'By Sep 30 we will reduce ticket-handling cost by ≥18%, measured against this quarter's baseline. Confidence 55%. If at day 45 we don't see ≥6% movement, we stop and reallocate the 2 engineers.'
scenarios.explain: Honest. Three numbers, a date, a kill criterion, a probability. This is a memo a board can govern.

scenarios.situation: VP says: 'We're investing ₹4 crore in AI to maintain competitive parity. The market expects this of us.'
scenarios.explain: Selling — using FOMO and 'market expectation' as a substitute for outcome. Board will see through this. Red flag.

scenarios.situation: VP says: 'We've identified 3 AI bets. Each has its own outcome, kill date, and rollback. Combined investment is ₹3.6 crore. Worst case, we're out 1 quarter and 6 engineers.'
scenarios.explain: Honest. Portfolio framing with explicit downside. Board likes this.

scenarios.situation: VP says: 'AI is the future. We need to act now or we'll be left behind.'
scenarios.explain: Pure FOMO sales pitch. Board has heard this 47 times. Always flag.

blocks.caption: Watch the trap happen live — and the fix at the end.

blocks.title: The classic trap: hiding the rollback
blocks.md:
Most VPs think hiding the failure case makes the pitch stronger. It doesn't.

**Pre-committing the rollback is the single highest-trust move available with a board.** It tells them: *I've thought about how this fails. I'm not going to surprise you in 6 months.*

The pitches that lose boards are the ones where the executive shows up at month 5 with a panicked memo asking for more time. The pitches that win are the ones where the kill criterion was on slide 3.

items.label: The kill criterion (date + metric)
items.detail: First. Without this, the rest is fiction.

items.label: The expected outcome (specific number, specific date)
items.detail: Second. The 'win condition'.

items.label: The investment (rupees + people + window)
items.detail: Third. The cost.

items.label: The narrative (why this bet vs alternatives)
items.detail: Fourth. Useful color, not decision-relevant.

blocks.instruction: Write the one-breath sentence for an AI bet you've considered. Format: 'By [date], we will know whether [metric] moved by [Δ]; if not, we [kill action].' Be specific about ALL four placeholders.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO statements about board AI communication that are TRUE:

choices.label: Pre-committing a rollback signals competence, not weakness
choices.explain: Correct. Boards trust executives who plan for failure.

choices.label: A confidence note (e.g. '55% likely') is more useful than a single optimistic forecast
choices.explain: Correct. Honest probability lets the board calibrate.

choices.label: The bigger the AI promise, the more the board will fund
choices.explain: False. Sophisticated boards now distrust large AI promises after 24 months of overpromising.

choices.label: If you don't know your kill criterion, list it as 'TBD'
choices.explain: False. 'TBD' on a kill criterion = no kill criterion. Decide before pitching.

hi-IN.title: Mahaul ka management — Indian board edition
hi-IN.md: Indian boards mein technical questions kam aate hain; *"why this, why now, what if it fails?"* zyada aate hain. Tu agar pehle se yeh teen sawal handle kar le, baaki natural follow-through hai.

en.title: What Indian boards actually ask
en.md: Most Indian board AI questions are not technical — they're 'why this, why now, what if it fails.' Pre-answer all three, in that order, in your memo.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 40% promised, 4% delivered
blocks.source: Anonymous board member, 14 board seats, 6 of them Indian SaaS
blocks.story:
CEO of a Series-D Indian SaaS told us in Q1 2024: *'AI will reduce our CAC by 40% within 6 months.'* No assumption ledger. No kill criterion. Just the headline.

6 months later: 4% reduction. Q3 board meeting: 'we need 6 more months and ₹8 cr more.' Q4 board meeting: 4.5%. Q1 2025: CEO replaced.

The replacement CEO did Q2's portfolio differently: 3 bets, each with a 90-day kill criterion stated up front, confidence at 50-65% each, rollback plan written. Board approved twice the budget at half the discomfort. **The behavior change was the reframe** — not the AI strategy underneath.

The original CEO wasn't dishonest. He was selling. The board, after 24 months of overpromised AI, is now sales-allergic. Honest framings are rewarded.
blocks.takeaway: Boards now reward honest probability + dated kill criteria far more than confident vapor. The market caught on.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: 30 minutes, board next week
blocks.setup: Vikrant has a 30-minute slot at next week's board meeting to present his Q2 AI portfolio. CEO wants 'transformative.' CFO wants ROI. Board chair was burned by the previous AI pitch and is sales-allergic. Vikrant has 3 bets and ₹3.6 cr.

coach.name: CFO-Veteran Vinita
coach.role: 30-year CFO who has seen 12 'governance' efforts work and 47 fail

stages.prompt: Vikrant's draft slide 1: 'AI will transform how we serve customers in 2026.' What does Vinita say?

options.label: Replace immediately. Slide 1 is allergen-rich.
options.explain: Right. 'Transform' is the trigger word. Replace with: 'three AI bets, ₹3.6cr, dated kill criteria, expected outcomes by Sep 30.'

options.label: Keep — sets aspirational tone.
options.explain: Aspirational tone IS the allergen. Board has heard 'transform' too many times.

options.label: Soften to 'AI will significantly improve...'
options.explain: Same allergen, smaller font.

stages.prompt: How does Vikrant frame his confidence on bet 1 (RAG over docs, expected -8% support cost)?

options.label: 'Confidence: 70%. Here's why higher than 50: we have prior internal pilot data, vendor benchmarks. Why not higher than 70: customer behavior on edge cases is uncertain.'
options.explain: S-tier. Specific probability + the reasons it's not 100% + the reasons it's not 50%. Calibrated honesty.

options.label: 'Highly confident.'
options.explain: Vague. Board can't calibrate.

options.label: Skip the confidence number; just say 'we believe...'
options.explain: Same vagueness, more words.

options.label: '90%+ confident.'
options.explain: Overconfident. Board has heard 90% before; the slide that comes after 4% delivery is hard.

stages.prompt: Board chair asks: 'what if it doesn't work?' How does Vikrant answer?

options.label: 'Pre-committed kill criteria on each bet. Bet 1 dies at day 45 if support cost hasn't moved 3%; engineers reallocated to bet 2. Here's the slide with each bet's kill date.'
options.explain: Right. Pre-committed kill criteria is the most trust-positive answer to that question.

options.label: 'We've planned for success; we'll figure it out if it doesn't work.'
options.explain: Worst answer. Board hears 'no kill plan = open-ended commitment'.

options.label: 'It will work; here's why we're confident.'
options.explain: Doesn't answer the question. Reads as evasion.

outcomes.perfect: S-tier. Board approves at full requested ₹3.6 cr; chair publicly notes 'best AI pitch we've seen this year.' Discipline carries forward to next quarter.
outcomes.good: Board approves ₹2.7 cr (75%) — half because of confidence-honesty, half because they want to see 90 days first. Worth re-pitching at Q3 with results.
outcomes.learn: Re-read the allergen list. Boards have heard 'transform/revolutionize/disrupt' enough times that those words now subtract trust.

points: Board AI memos need four lines: investment, expected outcome, confidence, kill criterion
The rollback narrative is the highest-trust move you can make with a board
'AI-first' / 'transformation' / 'parity' are board allergens — replace with dated commitments
Pre-commit your kill criterion on slide 3, not when the metric flatlines at month 5
One-breath sentence test: 'X by Y, killing if Z'

blocks.prompt: Write the kill criterion for one AI bet on your current roadmap. If you can't, you don't have a roadmap — you have a wishlist.

assessment.title: AI for Leaders Assessment
assessment.description: Tests judgment under realistic leadership conditions: vendor pitches, team-design tradeoffs, governance gaps, and board questions you cannot dodge.

questions.stem: An AI vendor demos a tool that 'reduces customer support handle time by 40%.' Which question best separates signal from theatre?

choices.label: Which model do you use?
choices.explanation: Wrong abstraction. The model is rarely the bottleneck; integration, eval, and operator workflow are. Asking the model name signals you have not done your homework.

choices.label: Show me the eval set, the customer cohort, and the baseline you measured against.
choices.explanation: Correct. A vendor with a real number can produce all three. A vendor with a vibe will pivot to 'every customer is different.'

choices.label: What's the ROI in year one?
choices.explanation: Tempting and very common, but ROI without the cohort and baseline is unverifiable. Vendors quote ROI from their best customer; you are not their best customer.

choices.label: Is it GenAI or traditional ML?
choices.explanation: Vanity question. The architecture matters less than whether the eval was run on data shaped like yours.

questions.stem: Your CEO says: 'we are AI-first now.' What does this concretely commit the company to?

choices.label: Nothing. It's a slogan until cost-curve and capability-curve shifts are named per function.
choices.explanation: Correct. 'AI-first' without a per-function statement of which cost-curve or capability-curve is shifting is a marketing line. Make it concrete or kill it.

choices.label: Every team must use AI in at least one workflow this quarter.
choices.explanation: This is what 'AI-first' usually decays into. It produces 14 vanity pilots and zero production wins. Activity is not strategy.

choices.label: Hire a Chief AI Officer.
choices.explanation: Org-chart theatre. The role can help, but only if there is a budget, a portfolio, and kill criteria attached. Without those, the CAIO becomes a slide-deck factory.

choices.label: Replace 30% of headcount with AI within 18 months.
choices.explanation: Specific but reckless. Headcount targets without capability evidence get reversed in month 9, and the trust is gone for two years.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are reasonable kill criteria for an AI bet at the 90-day mark?

choices.label: User-facing metric (e.g. resolved tickets per agent) has not moved 5% on the treated cohort.
choices.explanation: Correct. A specific, cohort-scoped, pre-committed delta is the cleanest kill criterion you can write. If it has not moved 5%, it likely will not move 25% later.

choices.label: Internal NPS of the feature is below 7.
choices.explanation: Internal NPS at 90 days is mostly a measure of who shouted last in a meeting. Not a real kill criterion.

choices.label: The team has not reduced eval failure rate on the agreed test set below 8%.
choices.explanation: Correct. Eval is the closest proxy to 'does this thing actually work,' and an 8% failure rate is roughly the support-ticket cost ceiling for most B2B SaaS.

choices.label: Engineering velocity dropped by 10%.
choices.explanation: Velocity is a process metric, not an outcome metric. AI bets often pull velocity down before they pay it back. Killing on velocity throws out winners.

questions.stem: You have ₹2.4 crore of AI budget for the year. A direct report wants to spend all of it on a single 'flagship' co-pilot for the sales team. Best move?

choices.label: Approve. Concentration beats diversification when you have conviction.
choices.explanation: Wrong analogy. Concentration in equities works because outcomes are continuous; AI bets are binary at 90 days. One bet means one shot at learning.

choices.label: Split into 3 bets of unequal size with pre-committed kill criteria; reserve ~15% for the bet you cannot yet name.
choices.explanation: Correct. The 3-bet portfolio with one slot reserved for the unknown is the canonical structure. It buys you a second cycle even if bet 1 fails.

choices.label: Split equally into 4 bets to maximise diversification.
choices.explanation: Too dispersed. Four equal bets at this scale produce four under-resourced pilots. Diversification without conviction is just thrift dressed up.

choices.label: Defer the budget to next year while you gather data.
choices.explanation: Costliest option. Capability curves shift fast; a year of waiting often means competing on a problem already solved by a vendor.

questions.stem: Your AI feature wraps a third-party LLM. Production has a 4% hallucination rate on financial answers. The PM proposes: 'add a disclaimer.' What is the leadership-grade response?

choices.label: Approve the disclaimer; users have been warned.
choices.explanation: Disclaimer is policy-doc theatre. Indian regulators and Indian customers ignore it. So do internal incident reports six months later.

choices.label: Block the launch until eval failure on financial answers is below 0.5% or the feature is gated to non-financial categories.
choices.explanation: Correct. Eval gates are real governance; disclaimers are not. You either fix the rate or scope the surface; both are defensible to a board.

choices.label: Ship to 5% of users with the disclaimer and monitor.
choices.explanation: The 5% bucket gets a 4% bad-answer rate too. You will have 200 angry tickets and a regulator letter before you have learned anything new.

choices.label: Ask Legal to redraft the disclaimer to be stronger.
choices.explanation: Same theatre, more billable hours. Legal cannot change the failure rate; only engineering and eval can.

questions.stem: Which two of the following are signs your AI program has 'centralised too early'?

choices.label: Every product team has to file a request to the central AI team to ship anything with an LLM.
choices.explanation: Correct. Centralised gating becomes a queue, the queue becomes a bottleneck, and product teams stop bringing AI ideas. The signal dies before the system can act on it.

choices.label: There is one shared LLM gateway with rate-limits and logging.
choices.explanation: This is platform, not centralisation. A gateway is healthy; a gating committee is not.

choices.label: The central AI team has a 4-month backlog and three product teams have given up.
choices.explanation: Correct. Backlog plus team withdrawal is the canonical 'too central, too soon' signature. The AI cell pattern was supposed to fix this.

choices.label: The central AI team runs the eval harness and shared red-team prompts.
choices.explanation: This is the part you should centralise. Evals and adversarial test sets are too expensive for each team to build alone.

questions.stem: You inherit an AI team that built impressive demos but no production traffic in 11 months. The first diagnostic question is:

choices.label: Where does the 'why' live? Who in the company can articulate the user problem this team is solving, in one sentence, without me prompting?
choices.explanation: Correct. Demo teams die because the 'why' lives only in a slide. If you cannot find a sentence-long 'why' from someone outside the AI team, the program is rudderless.

choices.label: What is the team's GPU budget?
choices.explanation: Common but wrong-altitude. Budget rarely explains demo-only outcomes; misalignment with a user problem does.

choices.label: Who is the team's manager?
choices.explanation: Org-chart anxiety. Replacing the manager without finding the missing 'why' just produces a different demo team.

choices.label: What model are they using?
choices.explanation: Architecture-tourism. Model choice was almost never the bottleneck for the bottleneck pattern described.

questions.stem: The board asks: 'What happens if your AI bet does not work?' The strongest response is:

choices.label: We have backed three independent bets; the largest is sized so we can absorb failure inside Q3 OPEX, and we will know by 14 September whether to continue, narrow, or sunset.
choices.explanation: Correct. Names the portfolio, names the size, names the date, names the action. This is the rollback narrative boards want to hear.

choices.label: AI is the future; the cost of not betting is higher than the cost of failing.
choices.explanation: Hand-wave. Boards have heard this from the last two CIOs; they have stopped accepting it as an answer.

choices.label: We will pivot.
choices.explanation: Empty. 'Pivot' is the answer that means you have not thought about failure, dressed up as if you have.

choices.label: The team is excellent; they will figure it out.
choices.explanation: Faith-based budgeting. Faith is not a control.

questions.stem: Your engineering manager wants to add 'AI features' to the next product release. What is the first artefact you ask for, before approving any spec?

choices.label: A list of user problems where the cost-curve or capability-curve has shifted in the last 18 months — and the one we will pick.
choices.explanation: Correct. The 80/20 lens. AI is not a feature; it is a way to attack problems whose cost or capability has just shifted. If your manager cannot name which curve shifted, the spec is premature.

choices.label: A draft spec.
choices.explanation: Drafting before the 'why' is selected just locks the team into the first feature someone thought of.

choices.label: A budget estimate.
choices.explanation: Budget without a problem statement is theatre.

choices.label: A vendor comparison.
choices.explanation: Vendor before problem is the most expensive shopping you can do.

questions.stem: Which of these is a real eval gate, not policy-doc theatre?

choices.label: All AI features must be reviewed by the AI Council before release.
choices.explanation: Council gating without a specified test is theatre. The council ends up rubber-stamping anything with confident slides.

choices.label: Failure rate on the 1,200-prompt internal eval set must be below 1.5%, with an attached red-team report from an external party, before any user is exposed.
choices.explanation: Correct. Specific test set, specific threshold, specific attestation. This is what an actual gate looks like.

choices.label: Engineering must follow our AI ethics principles.
choices.explanation: Pure values-statement theatre. Principles do not pass or fail; tests do.

choices.label: The CTO must sign off.
choices.explanation: Personal-approval gating produces inconsistency and bottlenecks. It also gives the CTO no defensible audit trail.

questions.stem: You committed to a 90-day kill criterion. At day 78, the bet has not hit it but the team is showing real momentum. What do you do?

choices.label: Hold the line. The whole point of the pre-commit was that day-78 you would want to extend.
choices.explanation: Correct. The kill criterion exists precisely to protect you from the optimistic version of yourself. Make the call at day 90 with the metric in front of you, not the vibe.

choices.label: Extend by one quarter; momentum matters.
choices.explanation: Tempting and seductively reasonable. The commitment was made by a less-attached version of you with better data; trust them.

choices.label: Cut now; if it has not hit by day 78, day 90 is wishful.
choices.explanation: Symmetric error. Cutting early throws out a real signal you might have at day 90.

choices.label: Add a fourth bet to hedge.
choices.explanation: Process injection. New bets take three months to spin up; the answer to 'this bet might fail' is not a fourth bet, it is the existing fourth bet you reserved.

questions.stem: Pick the two items that belong on a board-grade 'assumption ledger' for an AI program.

choices.label: We assume LLM cost-per-token will fall 40% by Q4 2026; bet 2's unit economics depend on this.
choices.explanation: Correct. Named, dated, dependency-tagged. This is exactly the form an assumption ledger takes.

choices.label: AI will transform the business.
choices.explanation: Slogan, not assumption. An assumption can be falsified; a slogan cannot.

choices.label: We assume the SEBI consultation on automated investment-advice does not classify our advisor flow as RIA-licensed; we have a 30-day pivot if it does.
choices.explanation: Correct. Specific regulatory dependency with a contingency. The kind of line that wins board trust because it shows you have thought about the downside.

choices.label: Our team is the best in the country.
choices.explanation: Marketing copy. Has no place in a ledger meant to survive scrutiny.

questions.stem: AI cell vs AI factory. Which scenario is best served by an AI cell?

choices.label: 200-engineer SaaS, 6 product lines, AI is one of three competing strategic priorities, you are still figuring out which problems matter.
choices.explanation: Correct. Cell is the right pattern when you do not yet know which problems will be load-bearing. Factory is for after you know.

choices.label: 8,000-engineer enterprise, AI is core to 4 of 5 product lines, regulatory load is heavy.
choices.explanation: That is factory territory. Cell scales into chaos at this size.

choices.label: 12-person startup with one product.
choices.explanation: Neither cell nor factory; just a team that uses AI tools. Imposing 'cell' here is over-engineering for the size.

choices.label: 1,200-engineer fintech with stable AI roadmap and known eval needs.
choices.explanation: Mid-stage; this is where the cell-to-factory transition usually happens, but the question asked which scenario is *best* served by a cell, and stable-roadmap is past that point.

questions.stem: What is the most reliable single sentence to put in front of a board audience that does not know the AI vocabulary?

choices.label: We will know by date Y whether assumption X holds; if it does, we deepen, if not, we sunset.
choices.explanation: Correct. The 'we'll-know-X-by-Y' formulation gives the board a calendar event to anchor on, and pre-commits to a binary action. It survives translation across audiences.

choices.label: AI is the most important shift since the cloud.
choices.explanation: True or false, this is a slogan. Boards want to know how *you* will act, not what the trend says.

choices.label: We will lead in AI.
choices.explanation: Empty. 'Lead in AI' has no falsifiable form.

choices.label: Trust us, we have the team.
choices.explanation: Faith-based ask. Boards do not invest on faith; they invest on instrumented bets.

questions.stem: An external consultant pitches a ₹6.4 crore 'AI transformation programme' across all 9 functions, payable over 18 months. The most useful question to puncture the pitch is:

choices.label: Which one function will move first, by what cohort-scoped metric, by what date — and what happens at that date if it has not moved?
choices.explanation: Correct. Forces the consultant to surface a kill criterion they did not put in the deck. If they cannot, the programme is theatre.

choices.label: What is your team size?
choices.explanation: Vanity question. They will name a number; you will be no closer to a defensible decision.

choices.label: What other clients have you worked with?
choices.explanation: Reference theatre. Their best client outcome is not your expected outcome.

choices.label: Can you do it in 12 months instead?
choices.explanation: Negotiating the wrong axis. The problem is not duration; it is the absence of cohort-scoped metrics.

questions.stem: Pick the two items that should always be written down for any AI feature that touches customer money, identity, or health.

choices.label: The eval set version, threshold, and date of last red-team test.
choices.explanation: Correct. This is the engineering paper trail that holds up under audit and inside an incident postmortem.

choices.label: A list of approved adjectives we can use in marketing.
choices.explanation: Marketing hygiene, not governance. Belongs in a different document.

choices.label: The kill switch — who can disable the feature, in how many minutes, with what alternative path for the user.
choices.explanation: Correct. A kill switch with named owners and a maximum time-to-disable is one of the cheapest, highest-leverage governance artefacts you can write.

choices.label: The CEO's quote about AI.
choices.explanation: Slide-deck filler. Has no operational value.

questions.stem: Which is the cleanest leading indicator that an AI program is healthy at month 4?

choices.label: Eval failure rate on the agreed test set has dropped 30%, and the treated cohort metric has moved more than the control by ≥ 3%.
choices.explanation: Correct. Engineering quality is improving and a real-world cohort effect is visible. Both signals together predict month-9 outcomes far better than either alone.

choices.label: The team has shipped 14 features.
choices.explanation: Activity, not outcome. Fourteen unused features is a worse position than two used ones.

choices.label: The company has been quoted in three press articles about AI.
choices.explanation: Vanity metric. The public narrative around AI programs collapses on first incident.

choices.label: Engineering velocity is up 20%.
choices.explanation: Often a side-effect of AI tooling but not evidence the AI *bet* is working. Confuses developer-productivity gains with strategic outcomes.

project.title: Capstone: Scope a 12-month AI bet portfolio for your CEO
project.prompt:
Your CEO walks into your 1:1 and says: "Board meeting on the 14th. They want to hear our AI plan. I told them you would present a 12-month portfolio. Make it real."

That is the entire brief. They have not told you the budget envelope, the risk appetite, the regulatory surface, or whether 'AI' to them means GenAI co-pilots, traditional ML, or vendor tools. Part of the work is figuring out what to ask back, and what to assume on paper when you cannot ask.

Produce a single document, no longer than 6 pages, that contains:

1. **The portfolio.** Three named bets, with: the user problem each one attacks, the cost-curve or capability-curve shift that makes it possible *now*, the size in INR (or % of OPEX), and the named owner. Plus a fourth slot left explicitly empty, sized at ~15%, with a one-line note on what would have to be true for you to fill it.
2. **The kill criteria.** For each bet, a 90-day metric — cohort-scoped, with a threshold, and the action you will take if it is not met. No 'we will revisit'; either *narrow*, *sunset*, or *deepen*.
3. **The assumption ledger.** Five to seven named assumptions, each dated, with a dependency tag (which bet it underwrites) and a falsification path. Include at least one assumption about regulation, one about cost, and one about people / team capacity.
4. **The org plan.** One paragraph: AI cell or AI factory? Where does the 'why' live? Which roles are net-new and which are reassigned? What is the governance gate, in one sentence, that you will commit to in writing?
5. **The board narrative.** Three slides, written as bullet points: the framing slide (what we are doing and why), the rollback slide (what happens at day 90, day 180, day 365 if assumption X fails), and the ask slide (what you need from the board, in concrete terms — budget, hiring delegation, a regulatory cover, etc.).

The document should be defensible against a board member who has read three AI books and one McKinsey report and now thinks they understand the field. They will ask: "What if it doesn't work?" Your document should answer them before they ask.

Be specific. Use real numbers, even if they are your best estimate flagged as such. "Roughly ₹2.4 cr, of which ~38% goes to bet 1" beats "a meaningful investment." If you write 'meaningful', you have not finished.

levels.label: Every bet, gate, and number is explicitly tied to a named user problem and a falsifiable assumption. A skeptic could attack any single line and you would have a one-sentence response.
Most bets are tied to user problems and have plausible kill criteria; one or two thresholds are vague or aspirational.
Bets are activity-shaped ('build a co-pilot') without user problems or kill criteria; the document reads as a slide deck rather than a commitment.

Assumption ledger is dated, dependency-tagged, and contains at least one regulatory and one cost assumption with a named falsification path. The rollback narrative names what changes if each assumption fails.
Assumptions are listed but not dated or dependency-tagged; the rollback is generic ('we will pivot').
No explicit assumption ledger, or assumptions are slogans ('AI is the future'). The portfolio cannot be stress-tested.

Board narrative passes the 'we will know X by date Y' test on every bet. Numbers are concrete; jargon is translated; the rollback slide is more credible than the framing slide. A non-technical board member could repeat the plan back in their own words.
Some sections are sharp and some lapse into AI-vendor copy. Numbers are concrete in places, vague in others. A board member would understand the 'what' but might miss the 'why now'.
Reads like a vendor pitch — adjectives without numbers, vision without dates, no rollback narrative. Will not survive a real board Q&A.

credential.title: AI for Leaders
credential.description: Holder can scope a defensible 12-month AI bet portfolio with pre-committed kill criteria, name a credible org structure, and present it to a board with a rollback narrative that survives Q&A.
